speechtext: I am not calling into question any circumstances as I do not think it is necessary for us to deal with procedure at this moment. speechtext:
I think that
which the minister has just said brings out the point I have been trying to make clear all along. My hon. friend now says that technically it is necessary to go into committee of ways and means on every item. I
say that the principle governing the imposing of any duty makes it necessary that that duty shall be imposed only as a result of a resolution coming from committee of ways and means, and that it can only be imposed where a resolution has been recommended to the committee by a minister of the crown who has the authority of His Excellency in the first instance to make that recommendation. The minister says that he thinks on some previous occasion, possibly with reference to New Zealand, we never had a committee of ways and means to consider the tariff items-

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
subsubtopic: COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER TARIFF RESOLUTIONS
speechtext: It was done in the budget.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
subsubtopic: COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER TARIFF RESOLUTIONS
speechtext:
-and if that be the case, I would say it is because no duties were being raised or any additional burdens being placed on the people or that the duties had already been considered in committee of ways and means as a part of the budget, or else that there had been a complete oversight on the part of all parties in the house as to what its rules require, an unintentional oversight and something with respect to which no question has been raised.
I hope the minister will now see that what I have been saying all along, namely, that we should have proceeded in committee of ways and means in the first instance, and that it is only when we have in ways and means approved the resolutions that we can with propriety legislate to approve agreements based upon those resolutions, is the right course to pursue. May I direct my hon. friend's attention to standing order number 60. This is not a question of procedure but a question of principle which governs the imposition of burdens upon the people. Standing order 60 reads:
If any motion be made in the house for any public aid or charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof may not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned till such further day as the house thinks fit to appoint; and then it shall be referred to a committee of the whole house, before any resolution or vote of the house do pass thereupon.
And section 551 in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms has the following, which is related not to the British procedure, but procedure in this House of Commons:
It is a fundamental principle that no resolution or amendment to increase a charge upon the people can be moved with the speaker in the chair; it must be initiated in committee by a minister acting on behalf of the crown.
1524	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
We have thus far in this house passed, or rather approved, four agreements, three of which impose additional burdens upon the people. We have done all that without being in committee of ways and means at all. It is quite true that we have been in committee of the whole for the purpose the minister has just referred to, namely, for purposes of discussion only, but not for the purpose of voting resolutions upon which fresh impositions in the nature of customs duties must be based. The discussion was general, but with respect to the agreement with South Africa, the committee was denied the right to do more than refer to the items in the schedule. We were told by the chairman that we might only refer to them; it was only when we came to the United Kingdom agreement and secured the general consent of the house that we were given the liberty of discussing them in detail. The step that we are now taking is the one which should have been taken at the outset with respect to the duties which appear in the schedules of these agreements; we should have gone into them all in the first instance item by item in committee of ways and means and had the resolutions reported therefrom; afterwards we would have been in a position to enact legislation based upon the items approved. The government has repeatedly said, referring to the treaty with the West Indies, the treaty with France, the treaty with Czechoslovakia and other agreements, that it is following the same procedure as was followed by the former administration in reference ito these measures. I respectfully submit that the government is not following the same procedure, for this reason; that in these other treaties to which reference has been made-I speak subject to correction, but I think I am right-additional burdens in the form of increased customs duties were not imposed upon the people and it therefore was not necessary in those cases in the first instance to go into committee of ways and means to have the house adopt the necessary resolutions. Those agreements related to duties as they were existing at the time, or as already mentioned the house had dealt with them in committee of ways and means when it was considering the budget; any additional charges or duties imposed by the agreement were in the nature of changes made when the house discussed the budget resolutions, and it was after the budget resolutions had been approved that the agreements were brought in and the approval of parliament was asked for them. It has been one or other of those two courses, but in any case if any additional burden has been imposed upon the people without the resolutions being considered in the first instance in ways and

means with a minister of the crown recommending them to the house, I can say without fear of contradiction that has been due to an oversight in connection with the rules, for which oversight all parties in the house were responsible and with respect to which no question was raised at the time.
With regard to this agreement between the United Kingdom and Canada and the other agreements, the question was specifically raised and the attention of the government was directed to the proper procedure and the underlying principles. The government took the attitude that there was a difference in the methods of procedure followed in the British and Canadian houses. In that the minister is entirely wrong. The principle is the same in both houses. It is a fundamental principle which is at stake, and one which should have been observed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
subsubtopic: COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER TARIFF RESOLUTIONS
speechtext:
With respect to the earlier portion of the remarks just made by my right hon. friend I am in entire accord. He has asserted that we are now taking the right course for the purpose of enacting the tariff schedules, but with respect to the latter portion, my right hon. friend and I must agree to disagree. I do not for one moment assent to the proposition he has made that w7e should have started in the first instance in committee of ways and means. If he will look at article 9 of the United Kingdom agreement, he will find that it reads:
His Majesty's government in Canada will invite parliament to pass the legislation necessary to substitute for the duties of customs now leviable on the goods specified in schedule E the duties shown in that schedule, provided that nothing in this article shall preclude His Majesty's government in Canada-
And so on. We are now doing that, and the only reason we are in committee of ways and means is in consequence of the United Kingdom agreement which calls upon us to implement it. We can do that only by committee of ways and means. I do not propose to labour this argument with my right hon. friend, because I am prepared to agree at once that he is thoroughly sincere and, if I may say so without offence, obsessed with the idea that we are proceeding wrongly in this matter. I wish to repeat: If the house had in its wisdom rejected the United Kingdom agreement, it would not be necessary for us to go into committee of ways and means. Therefore it would be absurd, prior to the house having assented to an agreement,^ to go into committee of ways and means in order to implement items in the tariff which are called for only if that agreement is approved by the

United Kingdom
house. I submit that we must agree to disagree. I believe we have taken the absolutely correct procedure. Having said that, I do not know that I can say anything more. I do not know that any good purpose can be served by our discussing the question as to what has been done hitherto with respect to the agreements and whether we have or have not gone into committee of ways and means. My right hon. friend and I are in entire agreement that it is necessary to go into committee of ways and means and we are here. That is the essential part.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
subsubtopic: COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER TARIFF RESOLUTIONS
speechtext: I am not any more desirous than is my hon. friend to delay the committee by discussing the matter at greater length, but it is one that may affect subsequent procedure in this house and it ought to be definitely settled at once. May I ask the minister this question: Assume for some reason it had become necessary to adjourn this house today, the Senate having approved the agreement with Great Britain and His Majesty's representative having given royal assent to that agreement so approved; would that agreement not then become binding upon Canada as law, and would not the changes in the tariff which are contained in the schedule which form a part of it be law? May I ask my ion. friend to answer that question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
subsubtopic: COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER TARIFF RESOLUTIONS
speechtext:
May I point out to my right hon. friend that we cannot in committee settle a question of procedure. The only procedure we have to do with in committee is a technical one having reference to the articles and the subject matter for consideration in committee. The question whether we should proceed in committee is one which can be decided only by the house.
May I say to my right hon. friend that there is nothing mysterious about this thing. If we were to proceed to adjourn parliament without having gone ahead in committee of ways and means and passed a bill based upon those resolutions, and if the United Kingdom agreement were to pass the Senate, be assented to by His Excellency and become law, we would be placed in this position, that while we had agreed in that agreement to do certain things, we would not have implemented our pledge by reason of the fact that we had not taken the necessary action in ways and means.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
subsubtopic: COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER TARIFF RESOLUTIONS
speechtext:
My hon. friend and I are not very far apart just now. He says we would not have implemented the agreement. But that does not answer my question whether what was embodied in the agreement would not become the law. He
has said that this house has proceeded simply with the agreement without going into committee of ways and means, thereby implying that we can make an agreement imposing duties without first of all going into committee of ways and means.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
subsubtopic: COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER TARIFF RESOLUTIONS
speechtext:
The bill would become
law, yes, but we would not have passed the necessary implementing legislation associated with it which we must pass in this committee of ways and means. My right hon. friend and I are not very far apart. The only difference between us, as I apprehend it, is that my right hon. friend says that we should have proceeded with ways and means before we proceeded with the bill. I am in direct disagreement with him on that point, and I think we must agree to disagree in that respect. I think logic is on my side for this reason:	If we had proceeded into committee of ways and means and had passed these resolutions and had then failed to pass the bill, what position would we have been in? My right hon. friend says that the answer is obvious and that it is only necessary now that we should go into ways and means because parliament has agreed that we ought to do what we are now called upon to do in committee of ways and means.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
subsubtopic: COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER TARIFF RESOLUTIONS
speechtext: When my hon. friend says that in the circumstances I have mentioned the bill approving the United Kingdom trade agreement would now be law, that means that everything in the bill is binding on the country, that it is part of the legislation of the country, that the duties there imposed are part of our tariff schedules.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
subsubtopic: COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER TARIFF RESOLUTIONS
speechtext: He has not said so.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
subsubtopic: COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER TARIFF RESOLUTIONS
speechtext:
That is what he said, and if the bill is the law that must be the case. But whether the Minister of Finance says so or not, after the bill is approved by parliament and assented to by His Excellency that bill is the law and the tariff is in effect as set forth in the schedules. But the procedure would have been wholly unconstitutional and against the fundamental principles governing in these matters. That point is very clear.
I am stressing what I am saying at the moment first of all because I believe that we would have had an entirely different view of this situation if we had proceeded in the right way, but even more I stress it because it is the duty of every hon. member, and of no one more than the leader of the opposition to see that the rules of the house are observed and that the right procedure is observed, and that fundamental principles are observed, and
1526	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
ilso to see if there have been mistakes made in the past or being made in the present that they shall not, if possible, occur again in the future. My contention is that we have already enacted these tariff schedules so far as this house is concerned, and going over them here and now a second time is a mere pretext in so far as the items in the schedules may be the same as those we have discussed. They are already enacted so far as the action of this house is concerned, and they have been so enacted without this house having done what the Minister of Finance himself says is necessary in imposing any duties or obligations upon the people, namely, being considered first of all and approved by resolution in committee of ways and means. We are at this moment in committee of ways and means for the first time this session, and we have not yet considered a single item. The whole procedure I contend has been subversive of the rules of this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
subsubtopic: COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS TO CONSIDER TARIFF RESOLUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall not
yield to my right hon. friend in a desire to see that the rules of this house are observed in every particular. We may differ sometimes upon the interpretation of a rule, but I am just as anxious as any hon. gentleman in this house to see that its rules are strictly observed, and I believe that they have been strictly observed in this instance except in this one respect, that we are breaking the rules of the house at the present moment in discussing a question of procedure here that ought to be discussed in the house. But I am not going to stress that point.
My right hon. friend draws an inference from what I said which he could not properly draw at all. speechtext:
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has just said that under the British treaty we extend to Ireland these privileges. I did not ask with respect to the British treaty; I asked with respect to the agreement between Ireland and Canada. Where, in the agreement between Ireland and Canada, is there any condition or any undertaking to maintain any preference? There is none. I should like to make my position clear, in order to illustrate what I sought to bring out the other day, and which was responsible for the change, in my own mind, as to the attitude hon. members on this side of the house should take towards the Irish agreement. That change was brought about because the minister was placing an entirely different construction upon the Irish agreement than we were placing upon it or than its wording permits being placed upon it.
First of all, may I say that at the beginning of the discussion on the agreements, I asked the Prime Minister if there were any undertakings or understandings with respect to any of them which did not appear on the face of the agreements themselves, and I was assured by the Prime Minister that .there were no such undertakings or understandings. I accepted his word for that, and in every action with respect to the agreements since that time I have based my action upon that assurance. I have been under the impression that there was no undertaking or understanding of any kind
between this country and either the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland, the Irish Free State, South Africa or Rhodesia which did not appear on the face of the agreements made between those respective countries and Canada.
The agreement between the Irish Free State and Canada is comprised in its entirety in the schedule attached to the bill we have before us. That agreement I studied carefully before this house met, in order to see what was to be given to Ireland. My reading of it led me to believe-and I am sure other hon. members must have come to the same conclusion; it is the only conclusion that could be come to by the reading of the agreement in itself- that it simply gave to Ireland an undertaking that no duties other than those which were imposed on British goods coming into Canada would be imposed upon goods coming from Ireland, and that no higher rates of duty would be imposed against goods coming from , Ireland than are imposed against Great Britain. That, and nothing more, was set out with respect to goods coming to Canada. Let me illustrate: If, for example, there were no duty on linen from Great Britain to Canada, for the period of five years for which the agreement would be in force, duty could not be imposed on linen coming from Ireland. Or, if duty on linen coming from Great Britain to Canada had been fixed at ten per cent, then Canada could not place a duty of fifteen per cent on linen coming from Ireland, because we had undertaken to see that no higher duty would be imposed against goods coming from Ireland. The clause is as clear and distinct as it can be.
Goods, the produce or manufacture of the Irish Free State, imported into Canada, shall not be subject to other or higher duties than those paid on similar goods, the produce or manufacture of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
That is the whole undertaking as set forth in the agreement with Ireland with respect to duties upon goods coming into Canada. In the light of the assurance given by the Prime Minister that there was no undertaking or understanding which does not appear on the face of the agreement itself for which approval was being sought by the government, I was prepared to voice my approval of the Irish agreement. But, what do we now find?
When we come to the bill to approve the agreement, we find that the government has done something with respect to Ireland which is entirely wide of, and apart from the terms of the agreement altogether. The agreement relates only to duties-no new duties, no higher rates of duty, that is all. By the provisions of the bill, however, the Minister of

Trade and Commerce told us on Tuesday last, the government was asking not only approval of the Irish agreement but approval of the Irish agreement plus the British agreement, in the one measure. Mark you, this is not as respects anything in the agreement itself; it is what appears in a separate bill. It is supposed to be an act approving the Irish agreement, but, according to the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, it is an act to approve of the Irish agreement, plus approval of the British agreement in its entirety. I say that is complete deception. Whether or not it was deliberate or intentional I must leave to the opinion of hon. members. To say that it was would not be parliamentary, but if that was the intention and the intention a sincere one, I believe it to be most extraordinary that the intention and the language, by which it was carried out, were not made known to the house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce before we were asked to support anything of the kind. Speaking when we were approving the agreement on Tuesday last, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
This whole bill-
The bill approving the Irish agreement.
-is based upon, allied to, intertwined and amalgamated with, or any other similar term you like to use, the British agreement. Every jot and tittle, every crossed t and every dotted i of the British agreement is in this.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I should like to know if there was occasion for surprise that, having accepted the Prime Minister's word with respect to what was proposed to be done in connection with the approval of the Irish agreement, and being led to approve it on the understanding that it did not increase or maintain duties, but simply gave to Ireland the benefit of duties imposed against Great Britain and being led to believe that duties would not be raised or new duties imposed I should change my position and ask the party with which I am connected to change its position when we were told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the bill not only enacted the Irish agreement but imposed the whole of the British agreement upon us as well.

My contention is that there is nothing in the Irish agreement which obliges us to maintain any rates of duty, so long as that agreement is in force. In support of my belief that there has been some endeavour to mislead parliament, I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to the sequence in which the different agreements were brought into the house. First there was the agreement with Southern Rhodesia, followed by the agreement with Ireland; that in turn was followed by the agreement with South Africa, and last of all we were called upon to deal with the agreement with Great Britain. The terms of the bills approving the various agreements are much the same, but there are one or two significant differences in certain of them, the significance of which has only just become apparent.
Article 4 of the schedule attached to the agreement with South Africa is as follows:
His Majesty's government in the Dominion of Canada will, in regard to the goods enumerated in schedule "A," maintain the margins of tariff concession represented by the difference between the rates accorded to Union goods in that schedule and the presently existing rates on similar goods when imported from any foreign country.
That was a clause in the agreement with South Africa definitely obligating us to maintain certain rates with respect to commodities coming from South Africa to Canada. In the Irish agreement there is no clause corresponding to that at all. There is no article in the agreement between Canada and Ireland which obligates us to maintain any preference, any margin of tariff concession or any existing rates at all. If at this time we are obliged to maintain any preference or rates of duty with respect to goods coming from Ireland it is because the government has gone outside the Irish agreement altogether and, by a

United Kingdom
clause in the approving bill which is worded differently from those in the bills approving of any of the other agreements, has done what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said it was the intention of the government to do, namely to smuggle the whole British agreement into the bill which we were being asked to pass at that time.
When we considered the bill approving the agreement with South Africa we found a clause worded except in one particular similarly ito that which appears in the agreement with Ireland. It reads as follows:
After the said agreement is brought into force, and so long as it remains in force, goods mentioned in the said agreement, the produce or manufacture of the Union of South Africa, imported into the Dominion of Canada in the manner provided in the said agreement, shall he admitted to the Dominion of Canada at the rates of duties provided in the said agreement.
The clauses are exactly the same in the bills approving the South African agreement and in that approving the Irish agreement, with the exception of these last words of section
3.	They will be admitted to Canada, the South African approval act says:
At the rates of duties provided in the said agreement.
If those words had been used in the bill relating to goods coming from Ireland we would have had and would now have no exception to take.

There is a reference to duties, which is the same thing. A schedule only sets out certain duties. "At the rates of duties provided in the said agreement; " that is as far as any act approving the Irish agreement should have gone, because it did not relate to anything else except undertaking that duties would not be raised or new duties imposed.
May I say this further. There is a double reason why in the act approving the Irish agreement the same language should have been used as in the South African agreement: it is that the language in the schedule itself warranted the use of the same language. Article 2 in the schedule is:
Goods, the produce or manufacture of the Irish Free State, imported into Canada, shall not be subject to other or higher duties than those paid on similar goods, the produce or manufacture of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
The act approving that does not include, as the South African act does, the under-53719-97
taking with respect to duties set forth in the agreement, but it inserts something which does not appear in this other agreement:
. . . shall be admitted into the Dominion of Canada on the terms granted to similar articles, the produce or manufacture of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
"On the terms granted," On those words, which we were expected to read in the light of the agreement between Ireland and Canada. and in the light of the Prime Minister's undertaking that we would not be asked to approve anything that was not in the agreement, we naturally assume that the terms there referred to were the terms of the schedule, that is to say, the terms of the agreement itself, and nothing more. Instead they were in the intention of the government quite other terms, namely, those of the United Kingdom agreement, terms of which we had no knowledge or suspicion whatever until the Minister of Trade and Commerce so informed us just before the division on Tuesday last. I say, Mr, Speaker, it is entirely in order, and indeed necessary, to bring up this matter at this point, because it affects the whole schedule of tariff items or rather tariff resolutions now before us. If the government continues, as I presume it intends, after what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said, to say that in approving the Irish treaty we were approving the whole British treaty, then all I can say is that the house has been completely deceived, and the country has been completely deceived as to the true nature and intent of the agreement made between Ireland and Canada. May I illustrate what I am saying in this way; there is nothing on Ireland's part which corresponds to the undertaking which we are giving in this parliament with regard to maintaining the British agreement in reference to goods coming to Canada from Ireland. The fact that there is not, shows that this addition has been made, not at the instance of the Irish Free State at ally but by the present administration for purposes, I venture to say, too sinister to permit of my mentioning them at this time.

In the first place I want

But I am going to crave the indulgence of the committee for a moment, if on no other ground than on the question of privilege, to reply to the last observations of the right hon. gentleman. The right hon. gentleman said that with motives too sinister to mention the government had deliberately deceived this house. In the first place that is not a parliamentary reference, it is strictly out of order. In the next place it is not true, and it cannot be borne out by the record. The right hon. gentleman has repeatedly in the last half hour indicated and also inferred it the other evening in a brief observation that he made just before voting, that he was deceived by the Prime Minister and by the government, when the Irish treaty was before the house. If you turn to page 888 of Hansard you find there the record of the introduction and acceptance by the house of the Irish treaty. I am going to read what the right hon. gentleman then said and what the Prime Minister said, and I will leave it to the house as to where probity rests in this matter.
Mr. Mackenzie King: With regard to the schedule,-
Referring to the Irish treaty.
*-I observe that for the most part its purpose is to secure both the Irish Free State and Canada against duties being raised against each other. It is protection as against the raising of duties on the part of either country.
That was his interpretation on the first reference he made to the agreement. Yet the Prime Minister deceived him, did he?
Mr. Bennett: I do not think the right hon. gentleman has followed the language of the schedule. The first article reads:
"Goods the produce or manufacture of Canada, imported into the Irish Free State, shall not be subject to other or higher duties than those paid on similar goods, the produce or manufacture of any other country."
In other words, no more favourable terms can be accorded any other country than to Canada^ Then, so far as the complementary article is concerned, it provides:
And the Prime Minister reads again from the agreement to the right hon. gentleman in reply to his question, enlightening him, calling his attention to the point. The Prime Minister reads:
Goods, the produce or manufacture of the Irish Free State, imported into Canada, shall not be subject to other or higher duties than those paid on similar goods, the produce or manufacture of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
Calling the right hon. gentleman's attention to precisely what was in it, yet he now says we deceived him on that.

But that is not all. Then the right hon. gentleman proceeded. I quote again from page 888:
Mr. Mackenzie King: It may be said, however, that, generally speaking, the emphasis is on protection of each country against higher duties, rather than-
And the Prime Minister interrupts, and sets him right.
Mr. Bennett:	No. I think I can put it
fairly by saying that it does not do either one or the other. It does, however, secure this preference to Canada, that we shall receive the benefits of the lowest rates imposed by the Irish Free State; and, conversely, we afford to them the rates, whatever they may be, charged against the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland.
Yet the right hon. gentleman says we have deceived him, says that he had not an opportunity of understanding the Irish agreement. Twice the Prime Minister set him right when the agreement was before us, twice he answered him, twice he corrected his interpretation of it, the same interpretation as he now puts upon it. The Prime Minister carefully, as a nurse would for a child, corrected the interpretation the right hon. gentleman put upon it. Yet he comes to the house today and says that this government deliberately deceived him, and " for motives too sinister to mention." What are the motives that he infers? AVhat motives have we? Everything that human beings could do has been done in the last three weeks to satisfy every reasonable question asked by my hon. friends. I apologize to the committee for speaking with a little heat, but is it any wonder? I ask hon. gentlemen opposite, leaving aside my hon. friends on this side of the house, is it any wonder, sitting here as we have week after week for six weeks, and during the past two weeks going over these items in the most minute detail, that we should feel at least somewhat chagrined when the right hon. gentleman stands up and says that "for motives too sinister to mention " we have deliberately deceived him, in face of the fact that the Prime Minister set him right twice previously when the Irish matter was under discussion ?
Now, coming to the point that the right hon. gentleman has raised, he says that I can show nothing in the Irish treaty that guarantees to the Irish the continuance of the preference. I have already answered the question but I will answer it again, and I appeal to the intelligence and reasonableness of any hon. gentleman opposite whether my interpretation is not a fair and correct one. We made no specific schedules with relation to the

United Kingdom
Irish. It was a broad and sweeping contract. The contract with the Irish was simply this, in plain language-and it could not be plainer than it is in the article itself. We said that we would give to the Irish the rates and conditions and terms that we gave to Great Britain. In other words, we looked at it this way when discussing the question with the Irish-and I may say that I discussed it with them myself and found them most reasonable gentlemen. We took this general view. The Irish Free State is now separated from the United Kingdom under Dominion status, whereas previously it was part of the United Kingdom, like northern Ireland. But we said that for the purposes of these trade negotiations we would look upon the Irish Free State as though it were part of the United Kingdom and northern Ireland, although in order to conform with the constitutional status we had to enter into this separate agreement; and instead of going into a lot of elaborate detail we merely extended to them all that we have extended to the British. Now, what have we extended to the British? Certain schedules, certain rates of duties and preferences; and furthermore we have guaranteed that in regard to schedule E the spread will be maintained. That, broadly speaking, is what we have done. We have simply said to the Irish, "We will give to you the same rates, the same spreads and for the same period of years." Could it be more clear or more definite than that? "But," says my hon. friend, "I don't see that mentioned in here." Well, the language itself ensures it:
Goods, the produce or manufacture of the Irish Free State, imported into Canada, shall not be subjected to other or higher duties than those paid on similar goods, the produce or manufacture of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
In the next article we declare that this agreement shall be in force for a period of five years from the date of its -coming into force and thereafter until the expiration of six months from the date on which either government shall have given to the other notice of its intention to terminate the agreement. If it can be made clearer than that, if the right hon. gentleman can suggest how it can be made clearer, I should like to know.
I resent, more than I can express, indeed, more than I dare to express, the suggestion, the unfair, unparliamentary statement of the right hon. gentleman, that from motives too sinister to mention this government had deliberately deceived. He had no right to make that statement. There was no ground for it. There has not been one moment during the past six weeks that we have not laboured, tc 53719-971
the point of absolute exhaustion, to give the right hon. gentleman and his followers replies as courteous and as full and complete as we could; and I may say to him that, in marked contradistinction to his attitude, many hon. gentlemen opposite, gentlemen, have come to me and come to the Minister of Finance in my hearing and, I know, out of my hearing, and have thanked us for the manner in which we have replied to their numerous demands. That I look upon as parliamentary sportsmanship. In the face of the courteous corrections which the Prime Minister gave to him when he put upon the Irish agreement the same interpretation which he now puts upon it, I invite the right hon. gentleman now to say whether or not he was justified in making that most unparliamentary and unfair slur upon the government and upon the Prime Minister and his colleagues.

May I direct his attention to the fact that in all that the Prime Minister said and in what the minister himself has just read, the Prime Minister was careful enough to speak of duties and rates of duties, but he made no mention whatever of any preferential margins or maintenance of preferential margins or of any of the terms of the British agreement. It was not only the part of sportsmanship but a part of the duty of the ministry itself, which it did not perform, to have drawn the attention of the house to the fact that these clauses had the meaning which is now attached to them if such was the meaning attached to them by the ministry. That is the answer I make to the minister. May I further observe that so far as parliamentary sportsmanship is concerned, we have nothing to learn from the hon. gentleman.
The first obligation upon a ministry, in dealing with any question, to say nothing of an imperial question of such large proportions and far-reaching possibilities as this, affecting as it does the relations between different parts of the empire, is to disclose to parliament the fullest significance and bearing of all that is implied. When I speak of sinister methods what I have in mind is precisely the kind of thing that was done when the ministry sought to carry through a byelection in South Huron

That request was refused and we were compelled to vote upon the resolution as an entity. The bill was introduced and when it came to second reading we asked that we should go into committee of ways and means at that time. We are now in committee of ways and means for the first time. I agree with my right hon. leader that we have violated every single rule of this house in the procedure which we have adopted.
In regard to the treaty with Finland, the treaty with New Zealand and the treaty with France, a special rule of parliament applied and continued to apply until 1927. The previous government carried out the rules of this house to the utmost degree, while this government has broken those rules.

This is dated August 3, 1931, and in the item, as regards the duty on' sugar of that classification, that is between 98 and 100 degrees polarization, the preference was reduced from 35-6 cents to 31.64 cents, applying only to Australia. This dissertation by my
hon. friend is one that we have of course heard before. There are those who take certain views regarding the process of estimating the standard of refinement, if I might say so, of sugar. I think this is the argument Mr. Deachman presented to the tariff board so very fully a year or two ago and I believe it would be most unwise to enter into an argument on it at the present time. May I reply to my hon. friend by saying this: This method has been accepted by the governments of Canada, the parliament of Canada and the trade for many years. It would be most unwise to enter into a discussion now as to whether some other process is better. This is our process and it has been in our statute for many years. So much for that phase of the question.
As regards Australia and the change that was made about a year and a half ago, that country, in the mills which treat the sugar cane, brings the standard of its refinement up a few degrees, I think it is two, higher than that normally accepted by Fiji, the West Indies and some other centres, I believe Cuba. So, in order to give Australia an opportunity to enter this market with some part of her sugar product, we adjusted the tariff item accordingly. That was most valuable on our part and to our trade, because we had an excess of trade going south to Australia to that which she was sending back. This gave Australia an opportunity for shipping some heavy and also valuable cargoes to this market.
The third point raised by the hon. gentleman was: What refinement was necessary beyond 98 degrees? It is very material. He has asked a technical question which, naturally, I cannot answer and I do not think the departmental officers who are here are qualified to answer it offhand. But I can assure my hon. friend that this sugar must be refined. Let him get that clearly in mind. The degree of refinement, however, is lessened by two degrees or, shall I say, two stages, if

Notwithstanding that there has been this discrimination in the tariff for years, this is the first time so far as I personally am aware that the question has been raised in this house. Inasmuch as this is an agreement, we cannot alter it in this house without the consent of the British authorities, but I think there is much merit in the contention of my hon. friend in that these rates operate to the disadvantage of those who wish to buy French books, and so far as I am concerned I am quite content to take the matter up with the British authorities and see if we cannot make an adjustment which would be more in conformity with the equity of the case. speechtext: Just a minute; I have a right to discuss this item. My reason for speaking is this: The other day when this matter was being discussed my right hon. friend was very clear in his statement that he was aware of the fact this agreement had to pass in toto, and that it was not subject to amendment. Under those circumstances we had every right to assume that these items, when we came to them, would not be challenged beyond an indication of the attitude of hon. members opposite. My right hon. friend was very clear in his statement that there could be no amendments to the agreement. To keep good faith it is necessary that we should pass these agreements in toto. We understand perfectly well that many items in this agreement are not acceptable to hon. gentlemen opposite. I would go further

But they understand the position, and in view of the statement of my right hon. friend it seems to me he is in fully as good a position if he takes the attitude of opposing the article to the extent of saying: Carried on division, which indicates that he and those who support him have voted against it.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, what my hon. friend says is correct as to my agreeing that so far as the items in the agreement were concerned we could not change them. They had to be accepted or rejected in their entirety. We understood that, that the agreement had to be passed as a whole. But we are through with the agreement now. The house is at present in committee of ways and means, considering resolutions involving far reaching changes in the tariff to all intents and purposes making a new tariff. Certainly we on this side have not deprived ourselves of the right, which every House of Commons has in committee of ways and means, of asking that with respect to particular items members shall show by their actual standing up in the house, whether they support them or not. It only 'bears out what I was saying before, that in this committee of ways and means hon. members should have had the opportunity of registering their position first and to make first the provision necessary to implement any agreement. Then, when we came to the agreement, certainly if provision had been made for the tariff schedule being adopted in its entirety there would be something to be said for there 'being no occasion to alter it in any particular.

I must say I have been surprised by some attitudes taken by my right hon. friend, but the attitude he now takes amazes me. What he says is that the agreement itself, it is true, we cannot alter, we may be opposed to certain clauses but it must go through as a whole, but now we are in committee of ways and means. My hon. friend knows perfectly well the reason we are in committee of ways and means, it is one and one only, that is to implement what we have agreed to do in our United Kingdom agreement. My right hon. friend is in an illogical position, I think he is in an unethical position. He says: While we will agree to these items we have in the bill itself, when we come to put them into effect in committee of ways and means we can oppose them. That is the position that my right hon. friend is taking, but this item has been passed as part of the schedule to the bill.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: SUPPLY-FARM RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
SUPPLY-FARM RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to speak at great length on this occasion, but there are some matters which I think ought to be brought to the attention of the house. Perhaps there is no need of emphasizing again and again the unfortunate position in which agriculture finds itself today. However recognizing as we do that the prosperity of Canada depends upon the stability of agriculture we feel we cannot give too much attention to that subject. About a year and a half ago I was compelled to move an amendment somewhat similar to the one to which we have just listened, and on that occasion I said there was grave danger of farmers losing their equities in their lands. In some quarters that statement was ridiculed. If not ridiculed, at least it was not accepted as a serious state-
ment of fact. There can be no question today however that the condition I described obtains. I hold in my hand a paper published in my constituency, and in it I find a list of lands to be sold for taxes. This is an old established community, a community that was settled fifty years ago. There have been tax sales at various times since then, but in very few cases was land put up for sale for taxes when the men were actually resident on the land. But today I find in looking over this list that some hundreds of farmers have their land put up for sale for taxes because it is simply impossible for them to pay those taxes. Again and again it has been brought to our notice that the low prices at which farm products are being sold make it impossible for farmers to meet their obligations. The time must come, be it sooner or later, when some steps must be taken to relieve the farmers from the obligations that have been incurred and have accumulated during the last few years. Some steps must be taken to secure that the farmers who are now on the land are enabled to remain upon it. What profit will it be if through the disposal of this land, whether it is taken over by the loan companies or the municipalities, men should be turned off land on which they have been living for many years, and then perhaps go and purchase another piece, perhaps one of these very parcels indicated in this list. Some steps must be taken by the dominion or by the provinces to ensure to farmers continued possession of their land; otherwise I do not see anything for it but a wholesale leaving of the land by those who are now on it.
These tax sales indicate one thing. There has been discussion as to the proper method of providing relief, and there are those who still strenuously advocate that relief should be given by way of work. I am inclined to think that we are driven to the necessity of providing relief by way of direct contribution. Ideallj' that does not commend itself to any of us. But so far as the municipalities are concerned at least it would be simply impossible for them to cany on any share of relief by way of work. Cases come to our notice from time to time that indicate the serious nature of the situation. Here is one, brought to my notice no longer ago than this morning. A certain man in a certain town was on direct relief. I was told that that man had securities in the way of mortgages on land, and land that he owned himself, worth at least S15.000. But he has not been able to collect a cent, and the result is that he is on direct relief. Now we could

Farm Relief-Mr. Brown
not hold that a man possessed of so much property should be allowed to starve, any more than a man who had nothing. But it could not be considered equitable that, in case times improve, he should be in a position to collect everything in the way of principal and interest on the mortgages that he holds. A lien of some kind should be taken on that man's holdings, he should not be allowed, if he so desired-we will hope he would not- to exercise his full rights without at least paying back the amount received by him for his immediate needs.
Let us consider another case that was brought to my notice, from the standpoint of the taxpayer. I was visiting in a certain town and there was brought to my notice the case of a young widow-

The case brought to my
notice is probably typical of a great many. A young widow of a soldier who was not able to secure a pension-

Never mind the young

maintopic: SUPPLY-FARM RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This young widow's husband had only been able to leave her a small sum of money, with which she was able to build a house to live in. She has no other source of income. Yet because of that small property that she holds she is burdened with taxes, and compelled to pay a share to support those who are out of employment today. The consequence will shortly be that her property will be gone, and she and her family will also be on relief. That emphasizes the fact that a tremendous burden is being laid upon the taxpayers, and we may very well ask how long those who are at present able to pay will be able to continue payments for relief. 11 is sometimes said that there is too much 53719-98
tendency to look to governments for relief. That may be true, but I think we have a right to look to governments for relief in cases where restrictions have been put upon people by governments themselves.
I want to call attention to a certain matter with which I have had to deal. Perhaps I will be criticized by members of the government for bringing this matter to the attention of the house, but I feel I would not be doing my duty to my constituents or to the people generally if I did not state the facts as I know them to be. Governments frequently make the statement that they cannot do this or that because of limitations imposed upon them, it may be by the constitution or by the demands of expediency. But we should remember that just as in war time things were done which perhaps would not be done under ordinary circumstances, so in times like these we may reasonably expect that governments will not hold to the rigid rules which might properly obtain under ordinary circumstances; and it is because I feel that the particular case I want to mention is one of those where it would involve no harm or injury to anyone to depart from that method of procedure which might have been justified in normal times that I desire to bring this matter to the attention of the house.
In one part of my constituency the farmers have for two years suffered from a plague of grasshoppers. A year ago feed crops were completely destroyed, oats and barley being a complete failure. They did manage to salvage a little wheat. This year the situation is very much worse. They have no grain crops and their potato crop has been also completely destroyed by grasshoppers. Shortly after reaching Ottawa I received a number of communications from men in my constituency, asking me to interview the government to see whether they could not possibly be induced to allow potatoes to come in from across the border in Dakota. In Dakota, I might explain, they grow rather extensive acreages of potatoes. In normal times they have a fairly good market to the south and so they grow large acreages, whereas we, not having a market, in some cases grow only enough for our own use. It happened also that in the north part of the state of Dakota there were some local showers which gave them a fairly good potato crop.
It was brought to my notice that potatoes could be bought at 10 cents per bushel on that side of the line, and later it became known that they could be had for the digging. I approached the government on this matter, writing to the Prime Minister, the Minister

Farm Relief-Mr. Brown

of Agriculture and the Minister of National Revenue. An answer came to me from the Minister of National Revenue to the effect that 10 cents a bushel was a price that did not represent a fair market value, and so forth. I took that to mean-

maintopic: SUPPLY-FARM RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think the hon. member will find that the reply was that there was a duty levied by parliament upon potatoes coming into this country. That was point 1. Point 2 was that we did not feel we had authority to make a regional tariff.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FARM RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In that case I will read
the letter I received from the minister:
Ottawa, October 17, 1932.
Dear Sir,-
I have been giving careful consideration to the representations which you made to me in your letter of the 7th instant, relative to conditions in the vicinity of Morden and Winklet, where there apparently has been a severe plague of grasshoppers which has resulted in the destruction of garden crops.
When you suggest that wre admit potatoes free of duty when imported by the residents of this district, I dare say you have in mind the action which was taken some years ago in connection with the importation of hay. I do not feel that this is a proper remedy for the unfortunate conditions in which the residents of tills place find themselves. It practically means the establishment of a sectional tariflE which is unsound in principle.
I can scarcely believe that our producers of potatoes are taking advantage of the tariff to the extent which you indicate. Does the price of ten cents a bushel for potatoes just across the line in your opinion represent a fair market value? I am not familiar with the prices of garden produce in the district but ten cents a bushel for potatoes would seem to represent distress selling and unfair competition with Canadian farmers who are producing potatoes.
Yours faithfully,
E. B. Ryekman.
J. L. Brown, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
As you will see, emphasis is laid on distress selling. Now my whole objection to the attitude of the government is that they give attention to that particular phase of the matter rather than to the distressed condition in which some of our farmers find themselves. That was the first answer I received from the minister. I received a very urgent telegram from one of my constituents, as follows:
Potatoes are nine cents a bushel across the line today. Many in the ground to be had for the digging. Potatoes in Manitoba fifty-five cents a bushel. Request Ryekman once more to lift duty for relief-needing farmers.
That is signed by C. W. Wiebe, a member of the Manitoba legislature, and the date is November 1. Although I had received an answer to my former communication to the

Minister of National Revenue, I felt it my duty to take the matter up with him again and accordingly I wrote, sending him a copy of Dr. Wiebe'b telegram, and urging further consideration of the situation. I received this letter in reply:
Ottawa, November 3, 1932. Dear Mr. Brown,

I wish to acknowledge your letter of the 2nd instant, with enclosed telegram from Dr. C. W. Wiebe, ALL.A.
I do not feel that I can add anything to my letter of the 17th ultimo. There are better methods of relief than the creation of sectional tariffs.
Yours faithfully,
_ _	E. B. Ryekman.
J. L. Brown, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Canada.
I admit, Mr. Speaker, that under ordinary circumstances the course we advocated might not be justifiable. But take the situation as I have outlined it: starving men and women, and horses and cattle dying for feed, on one side of the line, and abundant potatoes on the other side-potatoes that could be had for the digging. Yet the laws of our country prevent these farmers having access to those potatoes. The result is that they have no potatoes at all. Since the minister says that there are better methods of relief than the creation of sectional tariffs, I wish to ask him now just what proposition he has to make to relieve these people. Under the circumstances I have a right to ask what method of relief is forthcoming. These people will have no potatoes for seed next year; they have no money with which to buy them. They have lost their crop for two years and are in dire need of relief. As I say, I admit that under ordinary circumstances the minister would have been quite right in the course he pursued. But, Mr. Speaker, these are not ordinary oircumstances. We are not living in normal times, and it may very well be that we shall be compelled to adopt, not only in a matter of this kind but in many other matters as well, a course of action which otherwise we would not advocate for a moment.
I wish therefore in dealing with this question of farm relief to know just rvhat proposition the government has for relieving the people whose situation I have brought to the attention of the house. Not only that, but still further west in my constituency, where the feed crop was also destroyed, horses and cattle are likely to die for want of proper feed. In this same local paper which was sent to me I read:
Horses will die on straw.
Many cases of sick horses are already reported, due to a steady diet of wheat straw. Lack of oats and barley, and prohibitive prices

Farm Relief-Point of Order
for bran and shorts, will account for the death of thousands of valuable horses over southern Manitoba during the next six months. At present prices of wheat a farmer could afford to pay, say $5 per ton for bran, but $16 is out of the question. Must the horses die?
As I said, Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to speak at any great length with regard to this matter. The situation is clearly before the house. We will admit that the government has done much to relieve the situation, but I do not believe it appreciates the full seriousness of the situation that confronts us. It is easy for a man sitting in a comfortable office in the city to look upon these matters with a degree of composure, but it is not easy for those of us who actually know the conditions and who, when we go home, will find ourselves face to face with our neighbours who are passing through the hardest of hard times. Can we wonder that there is a growing feeling throughout the country that the powers that be have but little to offer in the way of actually relieving the distress of the people?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. On October 12 the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), seconded by the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) moved an amendment to the address to his excellency. One of the fundamental matters covered by that amendment was agricultural distress. I find upon referring to the amendment now moved by the right hon. gentleman and seconded by his chief wThip that it covers identically the topic covered by the previous amendment. Under the rules of this house, as exemplified the other day in connection with an amendment moved by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), the present amendment would appear to be out of order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FARM RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
on the point of order, may I say that the amendment now before Your Honour relates not to the past but to the future. It asks what the policy of the government is with respect to agricultural relief and what it will be during the months of December and January, at which time this house will not be in session. This information is asked for in order that hon. members when they return to their constituencies may be able to state exactly the government's policy. The amendment moved to the address in reply to the speech from the throne was as follows:
Whilst reserving any expression of view upon the merits of the agreements concluded at the 53719-981
recent Imperial economic conference, this house is of the opinion that the tariff policies of the present administration have seriously injured the trade of Canada and have intensified the economic depression, and that the government has wholly failed to afford a remedy for unemployment and agricultural distress as pledged by the Prime Minister.
The house regrets that, except the dole, the government has no policy with respect to the relief of unemployment.
It also deplores the government's obvious endeavour, by postponing the revision of the Bank Act, to avoid immediate consideration by parliament of the all-important subjects of banking, credit and currency.
There is in that amendment a specific reference to the fact that the government has not had any policy with respect to the relief of unemployment, but there is no reference whatever to the government's present day or future policy with respect to farm relief. The essence of the amendment which I have now placed in Your Honour's hands is the government's present and future policy in this regard. The amendment to the address contains the following: "the government has wholly failed to afford a remedy for unemployment and agricultural distress as pledged by the Prime Minister." Those words relate to the past, they state that the government had failed up to that time to implement pledges given with respect to the relief of agricultural distress, but I hope this failure on the part of the administration is not going to follow the lines suggested by what the hon. member who raised this question has said and be continued as long as this parliament lasts. While the government has failed in the past we hope that in the future it will try to carry out the pledges which have been made; at all events that it has some policy to deal with conditions as they are at the present time and a definite policy as to the future.
Without re-reading the amendment offered today it must be perfectly clear that it covers conditions of distress as they affect agricultural communities at the present time. But while economic conditions have cancelled the income of farmers and of people who are unemployed, and very materially reduced the income of those who are fortunate enough to be employed, still interest goes on. The fact that this condition cannot be perpetuated indefinitely or for any great length of time without bringing bankruptcy and ruin upon not only the farming industry but the nation itself, is equally obvious. It is possible that there are men and women engaged in other businesses, merchants, professional and business men throughout Canada, who adopt an attitude of serene and detached sympathy towards this matter. They are acting somewhat like the man who, standing safe upon dry land watches the straggles of some poor wretch overwhelmed in the turbulent waters, and contrasts his position of safety with that of the drowning man. The man who looks upon the possible ruin facing the agricultural industry and considers it as being of no concern to him, is about as stupidly unintelligent as the man who happens to be comfortably ensconced in the top story of a great skyscraper and, looking down upon the crumbling foundations, pities the poor chap in the bottom story. He says: How sad it is that that poor fellow will be soon in such an uncomfortable situation; he feels safe and unconcerned because he is far above the foundations beneath him but does not perceive his own peril. Business in Canada of every kind and all branches of industry are much in the position of such a man.
I shall not press this point, but I should like to draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, and to the attention of the house, the fact that when we speak of possible ruin and bankruptcy, we are not simply using terms and expressions-we are stating facts. The facts are these: not only wheat, our chief commodity, but almost every product of the farm in western or eastern Canada, is being sold at a price far below that which will meet the legitimate costs of production and leave a profit. These prices will not meet the actual out-of-pocket expenses which are necessarily and inevitably incurred. Take wheat, for example. The price received is approximately twenty-five cents a bushel for No. 1 at local points in my province. That price fails to meet the cost of the seed, the cost of repairs, oil and gas for machinery, the cost of binder
[Mr. Speakman.)
twine, and other incidentals in respect to harvesting and the cost of threshing and hauling in the crop. These are actual out-ofpocket expenses; I am not considering the value of the land or any interest which the farmer should receive thereon. I am leaving out of consideration his year's work and the value of his labour and management; I am leaving out of consideration even his taxes, and the interest which he should pay but cannot pay upon any debts which he may have incurred. It requires no mathematical genius or professor of economics to come to the conclusion that no business or individual could carry on indefinitely in that way without becoming absolutely bankrupt and ruined. These facts have been reiterated so frequently, stressed so often and challenged never, that one would imagine there is no thoughtful citizen of Canada who is not aware of them and concerned in their solution. The question will be asked, and it frequently is asked: what do you suggest should be done about it? Why weary the house with vain repetition? Why reiterate the facts which are admitted and deplored by everyone? I do not intend to shelter behind that bulwark so often erected and say: it is the responsibility and the sole responsibility of the government to find a remedy. I might do this, not only because in the government and there alone lies the authority and power through which and by which any action can be taken, but because in the government lies the capacity and means of knowledge and study which are not at the service of private members. The government has at its disposal the services of skilled and experienced men who have spent years in the searching and compilation of facts. In the Department of Agriculture there is a small group dealing with economics. These men have been employed because of their aptitude for and knowledge of this work. They are given the time and the salaries to continue their endeavours and explorations. I might well suggest to the government that, having these avenues of information, the responsibility is theirs, not ours. However, I assume for myself and for every hon. member of parliament some share of the responsibility. I shall not take the attitude which was taken so often by the Prime Minister when he was leader of the opposition, when in reply to a similar challenge and question he said:	''It
is time enough to prescribe when the doctor is called in-we are not called in." In times like these, when the very foundations of our nation are shaking, when hundreds of thousands of men and women are suffering, one

Farm Finance-Speaker'it Riding
should not stand upon technicalities. This is not the time to shelter ourselves behind the bulwarks of partisanship or of the particular position which we occupy in the house. So we shall do what we have done in the past, and offer what we can by way of suggestion.
I think the whole house listened yesterday with interest, with admiration and with deep feeling to the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stitt) when he described so eloquently and passionately the troubles and miseries of some of our unemployed and the magnificent heroism which they had displayed. I cannot say that I agree with all he said; I cannot associate myself with him in his individualism and denial and denouncement of cooperative action, but I can associate myself with him in that passionate plea which he uttered for humanity itself. I agree, as I think we all must agree, that wonderful heroism is to be found among those fathers and mothers who are unemployed and who are striving earnestly and sacrificing heroically to raise their children in decency and comfort. They are, as he said, the unsung heroes. But there is another body of men and women who might well be said to be unsung heroes. I refer to the farmers of this country, who, month by month and year by year, facing the inevitable, but fighting still; who, year by year, seeing the hope of profit from last year's work vanish, seeing in front of them an almost impenetrable wall of hopeless economic destitution, continue to do their best. Year by year, with hope unquenched, with courage amazing, they plough their fields, again sow their crops and carry on their farming operations. No wonder this is said to be a "next year" country. But even those men, willing to gamble against nature, to strive against odds, must ultimately reach the end of their resources. They are reaching it today and they call upon us for help.
What can we do? We cannot conquer nature; we cannot conquer drought or hail or tee vicissitudes of the weather or the climate. We cannot go forth into the world and raise the world price levels. We can do nothing of this. But we can do some of those things we have suggested and which I shall again suggest. As is pointed out in our amendment, the ruling upon which is suspended for the moment, one of the problems which presses more heavily upon the farmer than upon almost any other class is that of debt, that constantly increasing, pyramiding weight of interest bearing obligations. During these past years it is obvious that no average farmer, depending upon the product of his farm for all he earns, could pay the interest upon those obligations, let alone any portion of the principal. That interest, compounded every year, continues to mount up, and the debt, as has been stated in our amendment, has today reached an impossible point. In addition, the goods through which alone he may pay that debt-for he has no other source of income; he earns no wages-have so decreased in value that it takes an enormous and increasing quantity of them to discharge any portion of his obligation. Is that fair? What can be done? The Prime Minister very readily, and rightly, pointed out that it is not competent for parliament or the federal government to interfere in provincial contracts; in other words, that where contracts were made under provincial law, it was not possible for this government to interfere with or to alter their terms. I agree with him.
