Quite so. I was speaking at the moment on the question of the accumulation of debts. It was drawn to your attention that that part of my address was out of order. I understand, however, I may proceed in a general way. Therefore I shall leave that portion of it with this simple statement: The condition is obvious. In asking the government to take the lead in remedying this condition, we are not suggesting that it should transgress the law or should break provincial contracts or should interfere in provincial matters. We are asking this: In view of the fact that the situation has become impossible; in view of the tremendous potentialities that lie there and 
the effect upon the country as a whole, we ask that at the forthcoming interprovincial conference the federal government take the lead in setting forth the situation, and that in discussions with the provincial governments they together attack this problem; because unquestionably by a combination of the two authorities there will be sufficient power to deal with any matter affecting the welfare of our people. In respect of this debt we simply ask that the government take the lead in this matter; that they bring the provinces together in conference with the Dominion government, that each contribute its share of power and authority with a view to dealing with this matter courageously and frankly. The only way in which the end sought can be accomplished is, in my opinion, by a definite reduction of the amount involved. Is that fair? I think so, for after all when the money was loaned it had a certain value, and its value was what it would buy. Now any man who receives in return for his loan an equal amount of purchasing power, an equal value in commodities and goods, is being treated fairly and honestly, and is making a sacrifice which is slight in comparison with the sacrifice which is being made by many people in this country, including the agriculturists. Having said so much I shall leave that subject, in view of the ruling of Mr. Speaker, and shall proceed to other suggestions.
The second suggestion which is made, while it will not in itself cure the situation, is one upon which immediate action could be taken by the government in order at least in some degree to remedy the situation. The government, of course, cannot increase prices in the markets of the world. But the Dominion government has full power and authority to deal with our own currency and our own finance. While not suggesting that any change in our financial system or the amount of currency issued or the manner in which it is issued would meet all our problems and bring in the millennium, I do suggest that this is the most immediate and practical step which the government can take to partly remedy the situation which now exists. Other hon. members have mentioned Australia as an illustration, and pointed out the position of the farmers there. What Australia has done it seems to me that Canada can do. As a matter of fact, in other departments the government has recognized the situation and has taken action. Take, for instance, the question which has been discussed so frequently during the last few days in this house, the currency dump. Why is that applied? Because the government

Farm Finance-Mr. Speakman
recognizes that the manufacturers of Great Britain producing under a depreciated currency are able to do so at a price advantage as compared with the Canadian manufacturer, and therefore that advantage is in part removed by the imposition of a dumping duty. I think that that will be admitted by all to be the reason for the dumping duty; otherwise there would be no reason for the action that has been taken. It having been accepted then that the manufacturers of Great Britain are placed in an advantageous position in respect of their export trade by reason of their depreciated currency, by what reasoning can it be suggested that the same thing would not apply to this country? It is obvious from that very fact that depreciation or inflation, if you like to call it that, does not increase the cost of living or of production within the country to a degree equal to the advantage which it brings; otherwise the advantage would be taken away. So it is obvious that this is not only a practical suggestion which can be carried into effect by this government but one which, when put into application by Great Britain, Australia and other countries, has resulted in a definite and positive advantage to the producers of those countries. With the examples of those countries before us, this is no longer an untried experiment, no longer the fantastic dream of some theorist, but a practical matter which is being carried out in a businesslike way, and the results of which are obvious. Since it has reached that stage, not only do we not need to apologize for advancing the suggestion, but I think we are justified in urging the government to put into effect the same sort of measure here in order to give to Canadian producers the advantage which similar measures have already given to producers in other countries.
This question is of particular importance now to agriculture. In all the work that we have done in the last six weeks, in all the multiplicity of (argument and debate, we have had in view one thing-increasing trade within the empire, increasing the percentage of trade that we shall do with the mother country, increasing the percentage of our farmers' goods which shall be sold in Great Britain. And yet, as we have pointed out again and again so long as we refuse or neglect to deal with this money question, so long will all our efforts in that direction be in vain, and so long will our farmers be unable to take advantage of the very opportunities which we have been trying to give them through these agreements. There again we have a real and definite reason for urging
this government to try something of that sort in relation to our present agriculture.
_ May I suggest this? Even were there a risk involved, even were there some doubt and uncertainty as to the results, would it not be better to take action which offers a reasonable prospect of success than (to sit here in paralyzed inertia while agriculture goes bankrupt and is ruined before our very eyes? This is a serious question, Mr. Speaker. When I came down here from my constituency in Alberta I left the farmers there still hoping for results from their crops, still hoping that something would come from these agreements, still hoping that during the present session and before winter comes some action would be taken by the government that would enable them to carry on. We have almost reached the end of this part of the session and are preparing to go home, and what can I say to them when I go back? What hope can I offer to them? What can I tell them has been done during these two months to meet their situation or to provide against the future?
There have been the agreements, yes; but as we^ have indicated, unless the money question is settled, they offer nothing for the present. Only the other day, Mr. Speaker, I got word that less than half of the crop in my own district has been threshed, that throughout that whole countryside, on account of the inclemency of the season, more than fifty per cent of the crop was still in the stook, and that some of it had been stooked and restooked two or three times and would be left there for the winter. No bonus on wheat can help a man who has not- threshed his wheat, but in view of this calamity greater importance is being attached by our farmers to the smaller side issues. All they can hope for now is that they may get some revenue from their hogs and milk cows, their cattle and poultry. Their crop is a dead loss. Additional costs have also been piled up owing to the crop having to be handled over and over again, and the quality of the grain has deteriorated so that it is worth practically nothing; it will not be worth the trouble of threshing. That simply shows the increasing seriousness of the situation. The people there are waiting for something to be done-not simply waiting; they are doing all they can themselves, but they are hoping that something will be done by parliament which no body but parliament can do. So it is that we in this group suggest that parliament definitely and earnestly take action, whatever the risk, if any be involved, along

Farm Finance-Mr. Speakman
the lines which offer the most immediate prospect of relief by tackling this money question, and tackling it immediately.
There is another suggestion which we have offered and which we now offer again. As we go through Canada today, not only through our farms but through the large and small marketing centres, we cannot but be struck by the fact that the marketing situation is chaotic It would seem that everybody is doing what seems best in his own eyes. There is individual effort everywhere and no concerted effort anywhere. The whole situation, from a marketing point of view, is haphazard and chaotic. We suggest again, as has been suggested before, that to assist in this matter and to enable us to take advantage of the agreement, a law be passed which will appoint and organize a marketing board, a board which will have sufficient power and authority to bring order out of chaos and to direct and control channels of commerce so far as farm goods are concerned, not only for export but for the domestic market. Particularly should it operate in connection with our export goods.
As has been stated before and may well be repeated, we cannot take advantage of our opportunities in the British market unless we so organize as to control our exports, and to make absolutely certain that week by week and month by month quantities which can be absorbed are sent there. We should send no more and no less; the quality should be made uniform, and grading should be such as to be relied upon.
In short our suggestions are these: We suggest that the question of debt be tackled by the coming interprovincial conference, and that joint action be taken to reduce the amount of it. We urge that the government, with courage and intelligence, tackle the monetary problem, and at least give our farmers a chance by placing our money somewhat on a parity with our competitors, so that we shall not be labouring under a perpetual disadvantage. The difficulties connected with the monetary problem are just as effective as any customs tariff in keeping our goods from the markets of other countries. We suggest further that the government take the responsibility of appointing a marketing board so that the marketing of farmers' produce can be thoroughly organized, and so that they may receive full advantage of the best prices offering anywhere. Their exports should be so regulated that the right quality may be available in proper amounts in the proper market.
I am satisfied that if these three suggestions were carried out they would result in great

good to agriculture. I am satisfied, further, that if these measures were introduced the farmers would take new courage and new hope, and new life would be given to the farming communities. I am satisfied that if these improvements are carried out the good will be reflected in less unemployment, improved conditions and better business throughout all parts of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to prolong the session unduly without good cause, but in bringing before the house a resume of the needs of agriculture I feel that I am justified in taking at least a little time at the end of the session to discuss matters which have been spoken to by the two hon. members who preceded me, and which may be spoken to by others who will follow. Agriculture, although only one of the basic industries of Canada, is the chief one. If it is not carried on at a profit and in such a way as to enable those interested in it to stay on their farms and continue to produce the primary products, then there is a very bad outlook for the general industry of Canada.
It is most unfortunate that the matter of agriculture has not been placed before the house by the government previously in the course of this session. During the last six weeks we have dealt with tariff matters which benefit chiefly the manufacturing interests. Hon. members in this corner of the house, and I believe some hon. members who do not sit in this corner, would have been better pleased had the government of the day made a definite statement early in the session concerning its policy with reference to agriculture. The condition of that industry is so bad, as the two former speakers have said, that today it has become without a doubt the most serious problem that we in Canada have to face. The government has come forward to safeguard the interests of other industries. On various occasions it has stood behind the financial interests in respect to certain accounts so that they would not operate at a loss. I could cite one or two cases of that kind. Then, we hear that money is being loaned without cost to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company so that they may open their shops. As I have stated previously, many of the tariff changes which we have been discussing have been in the interests of manufacturers. Further, the exchange dumping duties have protected the manufacturing industry, and while the interests of that industry have been safeguarded, agriculture has suffered a double loss.

Without taking up too much time of the house, I should like to place on record the prices now received for some agricultural products. Today wheat is selling at a price lower than it has been in the last three hundred years. The situation is so serious that taxes cannot be paid, mortgages cannot be met, and bank loans cannot be wiped out. The banks consider agriculture to be such a bad risk that they will not make loans to the farmers. In that connection I should like to draw to the attention of the house an instance which came to my notice a few days ago-and may I say I could tell of many similar cases. A farmer applied for a loan of $50 with which to buy twine. He was reputed to be a first class farmer, had lived in one community for over twenty years, and had no debts against him with the exception of a mortgage on his property. He lives in very plain circumstances. However, when he applied for a loan of only $50 he found there was no response; not a dollar would be advanced for twine. The banks consider the outlook for agriculture so bad that they will make no loans. It takes seven bushels of wheat today to buy a 98 pound sack of flour. Oats have sold from five to ten cents per bushel. Ten bushels of No. 1 feed would buy ten pounds of rolled oats. Barley is fetching eight to eleven cents. Cream is about half the value it was in 1928. Hogs are selling at S2.40 a hundred pounds. I was informed the other day of a man who had sold a thousand pounds of pork and with the proceeds had bought the repairs for a couple of binders to do his harvesting. Beef is selling at from $1 to $2.75 per hundred pounds. Lambs are selling as low as $2.50 to $2.90; sheep can hardly be sold. Wool is selling at two to four cents a pound. As someone pointed out to me, it would take the value of two fleeces to buy a pair of socks. It would take a thousand pounds of wool to buy a decent suit of clothes. Hides cannot be sold. The other day in the south end of my constituency a farmer sent 52 yearling calves to market, and they brought him $460. At the same time eight beef cattle fetched $120. With such prices it is impossible for agriculture to carry on. It is regrettable to find that figures on the
cost side of farming have not been reduced. Interest rates, for instance, have not only been, kept up but are going higher, and freight rates the same. Such charges as commissions, elevator charges and so on are just what they were. I appreciate the act passed by this house a few days ago, brought forward by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) making it possible to cut elevator charges. They are being cut, I understand, very little, but it will help a bit. But up to the present time they have been either as high as or higher than in previous years.
To give some idea of the seriousness of the situation, particularly with respect to the farmers of the prairie provinces-I am not in a position to speak for those elsewhere-telephones, which are most necessary in the farm homes, are being taken out, I might say by the hundred, until a telephone is hardly of any use to those who have them because so many are off the rural line. Farm implements are selling at war-time prices, and repairs have actually gone up. Oil and gas are up; barbed wire is likely to go up, with the tariff increases on two tariff schedules considered the other day. Cream separators, as we have also beard, have been put up 25 per cent on two schedules.
The feeling is so intense in the prairie provinces that mass meetings are being held in many places. At a mass meeting held at Mannville, Alberta, in my constituency, a short time ago, no less than three hundred farmers were in attendance. When you get three hundred farmers gathered at any point it means that some of those farmers have come from a very great distance. I am going to read a resolution passed at that meeting:
Whereas, the present rate of exchange places the Canadian producer under a great disadvantage in the sale of his products, and whereas he is undersold on the world markets by competing countries, a situation only made possible by the exchange rate, therefore be it resolved that Canadian currency be immediately depreciated to the same extent as that of our competitors.
Another mass meeting is to be held in a couple of days at Kitscoty, Alberta, where I have no doubt that as great or a greater number of farmers will put in an appearance. In a manifesto that is to be presented to that gathering I read in part as follows:
The outstanding and major issue today is the relation existing between debtor and creditor. Creditors demanding payment and debtors unable to pay.
The creditor resorts to legal process, thereby compelling the unfortunate debtor to convert into cash any or all of his goods and chattels, regardless of the sacrifice frequently resulting.

Farm Finance-Mr. Spencer

If, as we submit, the present plight of farmers and others results from conditions over which they have no control, then they have not broken faith; are not shirking their responsibilities and have no desire to evade their obligations.
Then it goes on to say;
Therefore, be it resolved that as an emergency measure-
I will just give two items in this statement:
-the farmers be allowed to retain legally the proceeds realized from the sale of farm products:
1.	To the extent necessary to buy goods and services to continue their farming operations.-
Surely that is in the interest of the country at large. If anything is done to drive the farmers off the land it will have a direct detrimental effect on all business.
2.	That mortgage rights of foreclosure be
stayed unless deliberate negligence by the farmer is proven.	_
We approach this problem not "in humility and ignorance," but with understanding and courage, firmly resolved to secure Canadian economic reconstruction.
Those last lines, Mr. Speaker, seem to me to place the matter very clearly before this house, and to state in no uncertain terms exactly how the people, who are suffering as we have pointed out, feel in regard to this situation.
I was interested the other day in hearing the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon), say, I think with a good deal of satisfaction, that a large number of unemployed had been placed on the land-I believe he said some 66,000.

No, I said that included
people absorbed on the land-men, women and children.

I stand corrected. I can only say that I wish the Minister of Labour every success in his undertaking; for if they can be absorbed on the land and are able to stay there and get a living, then there is hope that conditions will improve. But I have great fears of the result. I have lived on the prairies for the last twenty-four years. I know exactly the conditions. I know what people have gone through and what they are going through today, and I fear that we are going to have a problem on our hands somewhat similar, maybe, a little smaller, because of the smaller numbers concerned, to that which we had in regard to the returned soldiers.

After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

When the house rose at
six o'clock I had just referred to a large mass meeting that was being called in my constituency to discuss agricultural conditions. They are directing attention in their manifesto to the big issue of the day, which is the relation existing between debtor and creditor, the creditor demanding payment and the debtor being unable to pay. They say that so long as this condition exists there can be no successful farmers' strike, no production control, influencing of prices, security of tenure, retention of homes, or even obtaining the necessities of life. It is therefore not surprising, in view of this situation, that they should use the language which I quoted before six o'clock and which I repeat now:
We approach this problem, not "in humility and ignorance," but with understanding and courage, firmly resolved to secure Canadian economic reconstruction.
These people are carrying on the great industry of agriculture and they feel that their backs are up against the wall. They realize, after twenty or thirty years' continuous struggle to make their homes and to improve them, that the day has come when they are holding them with the greatest difficulty, and many are being forced off their land simply because they cannot pay a dollar debt with a thirty-cent product. This has meant greater difficulty to the farmer than anything else, because in those parts of the country with which I am most familiar, I am thankful to say, the returns from the land, so far as produce is concerned, have been on the whole very fair indeed. But the frightfully low prices which I outlined this afternoon make it perfectly impossible for these people to meet their liabilities, and something will have to be done at least to relieve the situation.
Comparing the farmers of Canada with those of Australia, particularly the wheat farmers, we find that not only are the Canadian farmers handicapped in the selling of their wheat, on account of the exchange caused by the difference between the Canadian dollar and the British pound, but the Australian farmer, one of their chief competitors, has the benefit of a nine cents per bushel bonus.
The situation as I have outlined it has meant that the standard of living on the farm has been reduced, and if something is not done to stop the continued deflation that
[Mr. Spencer.J

Farm Finance-Mr. Spencer
standard will fall still lower and lower until it will reach the stage where we shall be ashamed to refer to it.
If one travels through the country at all today one must appreciate the fact that no building improvements are being made; that help on the land is being dispensed with on every possible occasion; and that sometimes children are being kept from school in order to assist their parents. The fact that labour is being dispensed with means that the people are trying to get along with too little help, the result being that weeds are increasing and farms deteriorating, and needless to say land generally is falling to an absurdly low price, though even at that price very little indeed is changing hands.
I wish to direct the attention of the house to a type of farmers we have who are putting up a courageous fight, men who, when they went on the land thought that they had at least a chance of making homes for themselves, even if they might not make money. I refer to our returned soldier settlers. I was delighted the other day to hear from the lips of the Minister of Labour, who has charge of the soldier settlement problem, that not in a single case would the government enforce collections in these difficult times if it meant bringing real hardship to debtors who were doing their best to make ends meet. I think I am quoting the minister correctly. I am rather afraid, however, that he is not as closely in touch with what some of the collecting officials are doing at this time as he might be. I am continually having brought to my attention cases of real hardship if the one-third per cent of the crop is collected from the soldier settlers, which is due from them to the board. I am not going to bother the house with many of these cases, but I will put two of them on record.
The first one comes from a man named J. A. Brown, of Westlock, Alberta. His total crop comprised 828 bushels of wheat and 870 bushels of oats. If one-third is deducted for the soldier settlement board he will have remaining 552 bushels of wheat and 580 bushels of oats. After deducting seed and elevator dockage, he will have remaining 480 bushels of wheat at 26 cents, or $124.80; 480 bushels of oats at 8 cents or $38.40, making a total of 8163.20. This man has school taxes to pay amounting to 854; municipal taxes, $22.45, and a threshing bill of $67.50, or a total of 8143.95, and if you deduct that from the larger amount it leaves him with a balance of $19.25. He has a family of four to keep until next year,

and he says in a footnote to the letter he has written me that ninety per cent of the other boys around there on soldier settlement farms are in a similar fix.

Yes, and many other words that the hon. member cannot. If I may proceed, Mr. Speaker, in connection with the unemployment issue, we find on page 1455 of Hansard, in the address which the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) recently made to the house, the following words:
I shall only summarize the situation by saying that the government has in course of preparation what we believe will be an appropriate agenda to submit to an interprovincial conference.
He is coming to grips with the unemployment problem at last.
It is proposed to call that conference so that it may conclude its labours between now and January 30, when the house will reassemble. At that conference it is proposed to discuss all those matters that have engaged the attention of governments, both provincial and federal, with particular reference to the question referred to by myself on April 29, 1931, namely, the problem of unemployment and how it should be and may be dealt with under the divided jurisdiction which exists in Canada.
These are practically the concluding remarks of the Prime Minister on November 22. That brings me face to face with the problem of unemployment insurance, because that problem and kindred subjects the Prime Minister admits are to be discussed at a provincial-federal conference between now and the reassembling of parliament toward the end of January. Hon. members who have been members of this house for the last few years will realize that as far as the groundwork of unemployment insurance is concerned, that was done two years ago. It was done by the Liberal party when in power, in cooperation with our friends in the corner of this side of the house. We had an investigation before the industrial and international relations committee each year for two years, one in 1928 and another in 1929, and as a result of those two investigations that committee came to certain conclusions. One was that we accept and endorse the principle of compulsory social insurance, based upon compulsory contributions derived from the state, the employer and the employee. That is the backbone of any unemployment insurance policy. That conclusion was come to in 1928 under a Liberal administration.
Another conclusion arrived at was that as far as jurisdiction in the matter of unemployment insurance is concerned, it belonged exclusively to the legislatures of the different provinces. That was number two. Number three was that when the census should be taken in 1931, information in connection with unemployment insurance would be secured and action follow the securing of that information. Number four was that since unemployment insurance was a big problem, more than one province should go into the system. One province would not be enough; Bvo provinces would not be sufficient, and the idea was that as many provinces as possible should take up the principle, hammer out the legislation and adopt unemployment insurance as a principle in industrial affairs in Canada. These are only some of the conclusions of the 1928 report of the Industrial and International Relations Committee. I might continue and say that in 1929, the next year, the problem was reinvestigated and practically the same conclusions were reached. The point I want to drive home is this, that when the Liberal party were in power, all the discussion in conection with this great problem was undertaken and completed; the groundwork for an unemployment insurance system was laid, and all the present government has to do is to take up where the Liberal party left off, show a little bit of courage, leadership and constructive idealism, and go ahead and evolve,-hammer out something that will be for the benefit of the industrial workers of this country.
In regard to an analysis of this intricate problem of unemployment insurance, there was one principle adopted in Great Britain. Across the border in the United States they have practically committed themselves to an opposite principle. In Great Britain they
Farm Finance-Mr. McIntosh

adopted a national system of compulsory insurance, and across the line-where little has yet been done-the feeling is that every industry ought to be responsible for industrial economic stabilization within its own limits; that every industry should not only be responsible for the economic stabilization within its own limits, but should adopt a principle of unemployment insurance by itself, then every major industry could be linked up with the other industries of each state, have the state come in and cooperate with those coordinated industries and thus give to that state and gradually to the republic as a whole a coordinated system of unemployment insurance that would work out to the benefit of the entire nation. In Great Britain they have accepted the opposite method; they stand for a national system of unemployment insurance which is backed up in a public way and to which the public is committed. But in the republic to the south of us they believe industrial insurance is largely a problem of private industrialists and that by getting together and cooperating, they, as large employers of labour, can largely overcome the obstacles in the way and effect a solution of the unemployment difficulty.
I have not time here to go fully into the question of unemployment insurance. One could talk for an hour on that subject alone, because it is a highly complicated one. But may I 6ay that it is recognized as a preliminary principle of great importance to have a coordinated system of labour exchanges right ;across Canada, and by manning those exchanges by experts, by having no person appointed to them except on the basis of merit, fey having the state cooperate with those exchanges and by squaring away the question of jurisdiction provincially and nationally, I believe there ought to be no difficulty in Canada giving a splendid lead in regard to this very vexatious question. I hope when the conference meets between now and the first of January, the Prime Minister, as promised, will gather representatives of the provinces together, and by discussion, by conference and by analysis of the industrial situation facing the different provinces in regard to this matter, there will be arrived at some successful conclusion and as a result we shall see adopted in this country' at no distant date a scientifically sound system of unemployment insurance.
When that problem is being worked out, the greatest care should be taken to safeguard the interests of agriculture. A system of unemployment insurance must be largely for

the industrial employees of Canada. That system should be such as to secure for them an adequate livelihood, to get for them from month to month and year to year work, a job or relief, and not have them wrongfully on the dole as they are now from one ocean to the other. May I read at this point a letter showing the condition to which unemployment has brought many a citizen of Saskatchewan? This letter is from a man who taught school for many a year and then went into business. He went to British Columbia and is now back in Saskatchewan. This is his story. I think the letter will depict better than can the language of any hon. member, the situation as it exists today in that great wheat growing province of Saskatchewan. The letter, which is dated Esterhazy, Saskatchewan, November 15, 1932, reads:
Mr. Cameron R. McIntosh, M.P.,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. McIntosh:
I am writing to beg that you remember me if you know of, or should hear of any kind of position.
I have nine children to feed, clothe and educate. Their suffering and illness for lack of necessities prompts me to write to you. Their present environment and condition if not soon improved is bound to influence their future as Canadian citizens. We are now staying with relatives who cannot afford to keep us, but as the alternative is exposure on the road allowance-
Note that, Mr. Speaker:
-we are compelled to share their little. I was compelled to leave Spiritwood last summer because my wages were cut down to a point where I could no longer exist. I sold my household goods to obtain funds in an unsuccessful attempt to better my condition. This is the first time in twenty years that I have been out of work. This is my reward after twenty years of service in Saskatchewan. By your acquaintance with me you know that I did not waste my money, but all I could earn I spent on my family. If it has been unlawful to raise a family I have no reason for annoying anyone, but for the sake of my innocent children I must exert every means to obtain employment and only experience could make you realize the abominable horrors of unemployment, the demoralizing influence of its agonies.
Will you please advise me of any openings you may know or hear of anywhere in the province or in Canada?
There is a letter, Mr. Speaker, that shows exactly the condition of affairs of many a head of a family in the province of Saskatchewan. I drew to the attention of the house the other day the fact that those seeking relief in the city of Saskatoon, and I believe it is true of other cities in western Canada, have to sign a document mortgaging their little homes, for which they paid $300 or

Form Finance-Mr. McIntosh
8500 or 81,000, as the case may be, before they can get one dollar of relief. From the standpoint of the state, or the strictly legal standpoint, to take the best possible security you can get, may be a good proposition, but looked at from the standpoint of national justice and common decency to an individual citizen who has done his part in the building up of this dominion it is a very hard thing to endure. To show what is going on, I will quote from a telegram I received:
We are asked to sign a document that on demand we should give a mortgage on our homes and chattels, also all moneys that are earned except statutory exemptions; further that any relief commissioner or its officials can enter our homes at any time they see fit.
Commission officials can enter a home and pester the life out of any head of a family in the province before he is given a dollar of relief. My mind reverts to what makes the state. I realize that the home stands for the building up of character, that the church stands for upholding the principle of righteousness, that the school stands for the development of the mentality of every pupil, and if I read history aright any nation worthy of the name has always stood for justice. But what I have described is not justice. It is the sort of treatment, however, the poor people in Saskatoon and other Saskatchewan and western centres have to put up with before they can get one dollar of relief. If they must mortgage their homes before they can get relief they must do it, because after all life is sweet, and before a man will see his loved ones starve to death lie will mortgage his homie and everything he has in the world. If he does not he will find himself on the roadside.
May I say on behalf of all those people who are out of work in the province of Saskatchewan and on behalf of all those who find themselves in straitened circumstances that I fully appreciate their great difficulties, and so far as I am concerned I have taken this opportunity to put their situation clearly before the house in order to urge the government as strongly as possible to alleviate their distress and remove the conditions complained of. Of course, I know what the answer will be. It will be constitutional in its nature. We will be told, as the Prime Minister told us the other day, that this is a provincial problem, that the dominion which votes the money passes the administration on to the province, and that the province must work out the problem as it sees fit. But apart from all those intricacies of law and constitutional government I wish to emphasize that the cases
which I have put before the house tonight are of such a nature that it is imperative for the government to do something to encourage people in such a desperate situation so as to make their lot in life at least a little easier.

Soldier settlers in North Battleford and Lloydminster are organizing. When we know that soldier settlers are organizing we realize that they have some reason for so doing, they are not organizing for fun. They are not organizing because it is a pleasure to hold public meetings; they are forming themselves into an organized body to get redress. They are organizing because they feel they must do that or later suffer. They are organizing because they feel if they did not they might be evicted from their farms. They are organizing so that they may demand justice and common sense action-justice from the department and common sense action on the part of the soldier settlement board. As far as their contracts with the department are concerned they feel that they have not been accorded by the soldier settlement board the treatment to which they are entitled; therefore they are dissatisfied. They feel that they bought farms at inflated prices, and apart from reductions, the amount owing is out of all proportion to the earning power of the land. They also feel that, as far as liquidation is possible, if their farms were liquidated today they would not pay their way. Debt piling upon debt, principal added to principal, interest added to interest. Moreover Mr. Speaker, the soldier settlers feel that they have done everything possible to pay their way. They do not think their present lot is their fault. They feel that they have a legitimate grievance, and they are going to do their utmost to have that grievance removed. They are not able to control the factors which .constitute the basis of their grievance. They have been told by the department that they must pay, and if they do not they must get out. Now it is impossible to pay, so they have organized, with two objectives, one immediate and the other secondary. They are organizing to meet the immediate problem of their debts, how to pay their way and stay on the land. The other reason for organization is that they feel that they have an objective to which they must drive on; if they

I have a return showing our trade with the Argentine, a country with which we did considerable business a few years ago. The hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) visited the Argentine on behalf of Canada two years or so ago, I believe, and he spoke in glowing terms of the possibilities of trade with that country. I have here the imports from the Argentine in 1930 and 1931, and I have them .also for the ten months ending October, 1931 and 1932. In 1930 our total imports from that country were 87,641,000; in 1931 they had dropped to $3,205,430. Our exports to the Argentine in 1930 were valued at $12,417,486 and in 1931 at $4,575,497. It appears to me that this business should have been encouraged in some way, as was suggested to this house by the right hon. member when he made his report upon his return from that country. What is the result for this year? Our total imports for the ten months ended October 31 are valued at only $885,723 and our exports at $2,650,688. We cannot expect Canada to make progress if we put up such barriers that other countries cannot trade with us.
I have one or two other suggestions to make. The first is that this government should begin to realize that their high tariff policy is not only a failure but is proving disastrous to the trade of our country. There is another problem which confronts our farmers and the people of this country generally, that is the problem of the spread in prices between the raw products and the finished article. A year ago the Minister of Agriculture made the suggestion that there was a possibility that some board would be appointed to inquire into the spread in price between our raw and finished products. This afternoon the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) gave some of these spreads, mentioning among others the spread in price in connection with leather and wool. Surely something could be done in this connection and I think the government would be well advised to appoint a board whose function it would be to inquire into these spreads in prices. Today our farmers are getting about one and a half to two cents per pound for their wool and they have to pay $2 per pound for the finished product. They are

hardly able to sell hides, but when they do they get about twenty-five cents apiece, yet they have to pay $6, $10 and $12 for a pair of shoes. Surely there is something the government could do to investigate these spreads, and if there is, I think it should be done immediately.
I should like to make another suggestion in connection with our trade commissioners and embassies located in the different countries. If it is the definite policy of this government to shut out the foreigner from trading with this country, why do we maintain commissioners at Washington, in Japan and in other parts of the world? Why does not the government recall these men until such time as we have a government in power willing to trade with the other countries? The expense of these offices would be saved. Unless something is done very soon for agriculture I am afraid that this industry, as far as western Canada is concerned, cannot survive.
In conclusion, I want to say this in connection with the tariff. I believe that any industry that cannot survive with a ten per cent tariff had better be allowed to disappear. Industries should not be maintained with the high tariffs which prevail at the present time. If they were allowed to disappear we would probably get reductions in the prices of clothing, machinery and a great many other necessities.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has been going through the greatest crisis in her history. It has lasted three years and is now affecting three-quarters of her people. If Canada is to get out of this crisis, whatever action is taken must be initiated by this parliament. The problem has now become so difficult that the ordinary individual is unable to deal with it. So far as Canada is concerned, the principal cause of the depression is the low prices received for the products of our farms, forests, mines and fisheries.
The prices of farm products fall faster and further during a depression than the prices of any other products. These prices have now fallen so low that it takes twice as much produce to pay his taxes, interest and debts, and he can buy only about half as much as he could previously. The majority of our people are engaged in agriculture and the prices they receive for their products constitute the bulk of the money which goes into circulation for the promotion of trade, commerce and industry in Canada. The prices received by the producers in our primary in-

Farm Finance

Mr. Coote
dustries largely determine the amount of purchasing power which the people of Canada may have in their hands. I do not think I could describe the financial position of the farmer better than to quote very briefly from a recent issue of the Farmers' Sun. The article states that the price collapse has cost the Canadian farmer one billion dollars and that the condition of agriculture is a national crisis.
The article continues:
Unemployment, decline of business and national financial difficulties traceable to the drastic consequences of falling prices.
Farming is being destroyed by the price collapse.
Canada's basic industry, the industry which supports 46-29 per cent of the people, which produces 58-3 per cent of the exports abroad, is being steadily wiped out.

If it were not so late in the session I would challenge your honour's ruling. I think what I have done is in accordance with the rules, as I understand them; however, I will be governed by your decision in this matter.

speechtext: The hon. member has the privilege of challenging my ruling.

I suppose it would be useless, and in the present instance I bow to your ruling. However, I think I am permitted to give some facts and perhaps I could give them a little more accurately by occasional reference to the article in question.
The gross annual revenue of agriculture dropped S174,939,000 in the year 192S-29; it dropped $369,034,000 in 1929-30 and $381,806,000 in 1930-31. That is a total drop of $925,779,000 in three years. The indices of farm prices for the present year indicate a drop of S400.000.000, which would make a total drop of 81,250,000,000 in four years. To correct that situation, drastic action is necessary.
While farm products have dropped to one-half their former value, prices of other goods have not declined in proportion and I find that the farmer's dollar, in comparison with 1926 when it was worth 100, will buy only 75 per cent as much retail food, 65 per cent as much retail clothing and 55 per cent as much household furnishings. The cost of agricultural implements to the farmer shows that the price of implements has not dropped more than a fraction of the drop in the prices of farm products. We find that ploughs still have 100 per cent, drills, 98.4 per cent, wagons
97.1 per cent and binders 96.3 per cent of their 1926 values. In order to purchase any of these implements, it takes twice as many farm products at prevailing prices as it did in 1926. I was told this fall by one merchant in my home town that the price of binders which he handled had dropped 85. This was a 8300 binder and he said that that was the equivalent of a drop of eight cents in the price of a 85 pair of shoes.
To sum up again, I would say that the unequal fall in farm prices has doubled the farmer's debts, taxes, interest,' insurance premiums and all fixed charges. It has certainly cut the purchasing power of his products anywhere from 30 to 60 per cent, depending upon the class of goods he has to buy with his products. In fact, if he pays all these fixed charges, he will not have any purchasing power at all and he will have to live on what he produces on the farm. The women will have to go back to the spinning wheel, or the farmer's family will have to go without clothes. The result is that farm women today are canning their own vegetables; they are canning fruit, poultry, meat. They are doing their best to provide a living for their families off what they produce on the farm. In some cases they are taking old dresses out of the ragbag and mending them because they cannot buy new ones. The farmers are today buying very little. Most of them are down to the very minimum. The fact that they are not buying is not because they do noit want to buy, but because they have not the wherewithal. They are skimping and retrenching in every possible way; they are working harder and getting less than they ever did before. Because the farmers are able to buy so little, there is unemployment in retail and wholesale stores, in our factories and on our railways. One reason that there are idle canning factories in Ontario is that the western farmer is no longer able to buy canned goods. If he has any canned goods, the women have to can them themselves. One-fifth of our people are out of work. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) told us that 800,000 people were on relief, and I am sure another 1,000,000 are out of work and being kept by their relatives or living on what little they have left.
Where does the hon. gentleman get those figures?
The figure of 800,000 was given by the minister. The other figures were given to me in one case by a professor of economics who made this estimate.

That is hopeless.
Farm Finance-Mr. Coote
Well, those who are out of work and not on direct relief would, with their dependents, make that many.
The 800,000 include dependents.

But those are only people who are on direct relief from municipalities, provincial governments or the federal government. There are hundreds of thousands who are out of work, who are still living on their means or being kept by their relatives. No doubt there are several hundred thousand young men and women who have finished their schooling and who want to go to work, but for whom there is no work. This number would be included in the million people that I suggested a few minutes ago as being out of work. All those people are existing on a reduced standard of living. Under such conditions they must reduce it.
The situation is becoming so bad that action must be taken at once. If not, the bonds of some of our municipalities, many of them in fact, to the extent of many millions of dollars are bound to go into default. The farmer's power to pay taxes to meet interest on bonds is not there. The investments of loan, trust and insurance companies is bound to be affected; it cannot be avoided. Even the investments of our governments are affected and in fact the whole financial structure of the country is affected by the low price of farm products. The situation demands prompt action and I am glad to hear that we are to have a conference of provincial premiers to be called probably in January. I would suggest that when this premiers' conference is called, they should consider action on similar lines to that which was taken in Australia a year and a half ago at what was known as the premiers' conference, when it was agreed that all the states should introduce legislation to reduce interest rates on existing mortgages and agreements of sale by 22i per cent of the existing rate. The banks also agreed to reduce interest on their loans by one per cent and interest on deposits by one per cent. It was agreed that a bonus on wheat amounting to
pence per bushel should be paid on last year's crop. It was also agreed at this conference that the exporter should be helped by depreciation in Australian currency. The conference also agreed to a conversion of the entire internal bonded indebtedness of the commonwealth and of the Australian states at a reduction of 224 per cent of the existing rates. This conversion was carried out shortly afterwards, 97 per cent of the bonds being voluntarily converted and the remaining three per cent being converted by legislation. That

effected a saving of $16,000,000 annually to the commonwealth and the various states. The greatest benefit has come to Australia through a depreciation of her currency. I know some people would immediately say that such a course would ruin the credit of Canada; that her bonds would not be saleable after such an operation as that. I find in the Commerce of the Nation, in a recent issue this dispatch:
New South Wales, Australia, conversion loan of some $50,000,000 launched under aegis of Commonwealth government was taken up in London market within half an hour.
That was a foreign loan.
Will reduce former interest of 5i per cent to nominal rate of 3J per cent though over-all yield of four per cent will be realized by investors. Saving estimated at over $2,000,000 per annum.
Canada's government has made great efforts to maintain her credit on a high standing with foreign countries, but I doubt very much whether after all this effort Canada could secure a bond issue in any foreign country at a net rate of four per cent and that is what the state of New South Wales has recently been able to do.
May I also mention this in passing:
British government announces new conversion loan involving $400,000,000, causing sharp rise in government securities. British treasury two per cent bonds totalling $200,000,000 undei'-written in record time in city of London.
Great Britain quite frankly abandoned the gold standard a year ago last September. The result is very low interest rates in that country, as evidenced by the fact that the British government is able to sell $200,000,000 of treasury notes at a rate of two per cent, while in Canada our government pays the banks four per cent on treasury notes.
Coming back to Australia and the depreciation of her currency which was agreed upon at that conference, I find in a recent issue of the Ottawa Journal a splendid editorial which is headed: "An Australian Recovery."
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that you will not allow me to read this editorial. I would just say that it goes on to make some very favourable comment on the Australian situation. It says that there is a certain amount of criticism in Australian papers about the action that has been taken, but that the criticism has arisen mainly on the part of party politicians. Perhaps on some later occasion I may be able to read it.
I have another editorial here from the Leader-Post of Regina, dated November 8, and headed "Australia Reports Recovery." It goes on to make some very complimentary remarks on the Australian situation and winds

Farm Finance-Mr. Coote
up by saying that business and trade in Australia are coming to life as a result of the policies put into operation, and says that this does not appear to be happening in Canada, and it asks: Have we been following the wrong path?
I read in a recent dispatch that Australia this year has set aside one and a quarter million pounds for the purpose of paying a bonus to wheat growers. They also propose to pay a bounty of one pound per acre-I give that figure subject to correction-for fertilizer. They also propose to make a reduction in the land tax in Australia.
At the present time the currency of Australia is depreciated sixty per cent as compared with that of Canada. Some bankers in Australia have advocated that that depreciation should be even more than sixty per cent so as to assist the Australian exporters to continue in business. I should like to say a word or two on the recent action of the Prime Minister by which he indulged in a small measure of inflation I refer to his action in regard to the sale of $35,000,000 of treasury notes to the Canadian banks at four per cent.
Three per cent.

He was borrowing from the Canadian banks at four per cent. The Canadian banks then borrowed $35,000,000 from the Finance department at three per cent, using these treasury notes as security. This is unquestionably a measure of inflation, and I would ask the house to note that the basis of that inflation was money made by the printing press.
Does the hon. member say that commodity prices have risen since that action was taken?

No, commodity prices have not risen. I was just going to bring out that point. There will be very little increase in commodity prices from this small measure of inflation. This $35,000,000 in the vaults of the banks does furnish a basis for issuing bank credit to the amount of $300,000,000 if the banks care to issue that amount of credit, and can find customers who will borrow from them and give them satisfactory security. The banks do not loan to a producer unless the price of the commodity he produces is at such a level that the banker can naturally expect his customer to secure the cost of production plus a profit equal to the interest charge on the loan. When the price of farm products is so low that the banker believes that the farmer cannot get sufficient for his products to repay the bank _oan with interest, he does
not make the loan. If the banks are to be able to use that $35,000,000 as a basis for issuing credit in Canada under our present system, we must do something to increase commodity prices. When commodity prices are increased to the point where the banks think that the producer can make a profit sufficient to pay the interest on the loan, the banks will again begin to loan to the producer. So the great problem facing us today is to raise commodity prices. I should like to quote a statement made by Sir William Beveridge, who is director of the London School of Economics. The statement is taken from The World's Economic Crisis and the Way of Escape, published in London last year. Speaking of prices, Sir William Beveridge says that there are three different movements of prices.
I shall not refer to the first two because my time is limited:
There may be, third, a general movement of prices initiated from the side of money. What we have in this crisis is a change of this third kind, a fall of prices representing deflation of money. That is what we are concerned with in the first instance.
I would direct the attention of the house to that statement of Sir William Beveridge, that what we have in this case is a fall in prices representing deflation of money. He says on the following page:
The fall of prices with which we are concerned is initiated from the side of money. It is a deflationary fall of unexampled violence.
Sir William Beveridge is an able and noted economist, and is generally regarded, I think, as orthodox. He is authority for the statement that the fall of prices with which we are concerned today is initiated from the side of money, and that it is a deflationary fall of unexampled violence. Every economist that I have read for the last year agrees that tjhe world today is suffering from a depression that has been caused by a deflation of prices, and there you have Sir William Beveridge's statement that the cause of the fall of prices was the deflation of money. If we are going to raise prices we must raise them through monetary action. If the fall in prices was caused by deflation, the way to raise prices is by inflation.
Bringing prices back to normal?

Yes. It is sometimes called reflation. Our prices are fifty per cent below normal, and the people who are depending on the price of their commodities to meet their debts and living costs are simply unable to meet them and are drifting fast into bankruptcy.
Farm Finance,-Mr. Coote

I was very sorry that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) today was ruled out of order because I think it was a good amendment. It referred first to the question of debts, to which I have made a very brief reference. Then he went on to deal with the question of a wheat bonus. I should like to say a few words on that matter.
First of all, why should there be a wheat bonus? Because wheat is the most important item in our whole national economy. It is our greatest item of export. It furnishes employment for more of our people than any other commodity. Next to minerals it furnishes the greatest amount of traffic and traffic earnings for our railways. We had a bonus on wheat last year. There must have been very good reasons for that, and the reasons that existed then are still in force today. As a matter of fact, there is more reason for the wheat bonus today than there was a year ago. One of our chief competitors is Australia. Last year the Australian farmer got a bonus of nine cents a bushel as compared with five cents a bushel in Canada. Australia has already set aside one and a quarter million pounds to bonus her farmers this year but this government is doing nothing to provide a bonus. I want to assure the house that our farmers are badly in need of the bonus. I have a telegram here which I received from some people in my constituency a short time ago. It says:
Large meeting of your constituents held at Blackie on Monday night strongly urge that price of grain and general conditions of the fanner necessitate this year a bonus on grain production by the Dominion government.
I should like to give hon. members some idea of the position in which many of our wheat growers find themselves. Any farmer who is able to produce No. 1 wheat can get today about 26 cents a bushel, a price which is much less than the cost of production. However all our wheat does not grade No. 1.
I have before me a clipping from a Calgary newspaper which was sent to me recently. It is sent from Cardston, Alberta, and is dated October 25:
A. W. Zeigler of Cardston, Friday took settlement for his good crop of fall wheat, which averaged 33 bushels to the acre over the whole field.
Wheat in Cardston was selling at 28J cents a bushel locally. The elevator people deducted C cents a bushel because it was fall wheat. Then they said it was smutty so took off another 6 cents a bushel. They then decided it was tough, and so extracted another 6 cents from the selling price.
It had already cost Mr. Zeigler 7 cents a bushel for twine and threshing, and it took 3 
cents a bushel for hauling to the elevator. This amounted to 28 cents a bushel, leaving Mr. Zeigler exactly J cent a bushel to cover his years work, his seed, ploughing, drilling, cultivating, and a long summer's anxiety about hail, drought and grasshoppers, with deductions for the herd of collectors who saw the field of wheat grow into maturity.
I would not like hon. members to think that all farmers in Alberta are receiving only one-half cent per bushel for their wheat. But even those who received 27 cents at the elevator, after paying for threshing and hauling, twine, stooking, groceries for feeding the stookers, and binder repairs, would have practically nothing left.

acquainted with farming as to the necessity of raising farm prices. Next we come to the question of how to raise them. As the prices of grain, cattle, hogs and I think poultry, are all on an export basis, the way to raise them is to allow our currency to depreciate in outside countries as was done by Australia. This creates a premium on foreign exchange, and as the exportable surplus of these products is sold for foreign exchange the prices will be raised in terms of Canadian currency. If the price of our exports is raised this will raise the price of that part consumed at home, because, unfortunately, the surplus exported fixes the price of practically all farm produce. Today the British pound is worth only about $3.78 in Canada, when it should be worth at least $4.87. We are losing $20 on every steer exported; $2.80 on a bacon hog; 7 cents a pound on turkeys; 7J cents a dozen on eggs and 19 cents a bushel on wheat. These figures are taken from the evidence given by exporters to a correspondent of the Country Guide. I do not think Canadian farmers will be getting a square deal even when the pound is worth $4.87 in Canada. The British pound is worth about $6.10 in Australia. I learn that

definite action to raise the exchange rate is to be taken by New Zealand, so that the British pound may be worth as much in New Zealand as it is in Australia.
I put this question to hon. members in the house, and particularly hon. members opposite: How are our farmers going to ship butter to England to compete with New Zealand? Absolutely impossible. The countries with which we compete have a great exchange advantage over us. Australia, New Zealand, the Argentine, Denmark, Sweden and Norway enjoy this advantage. Compared with us they have depreciated their currency from 25 to 50 per cent. They can undersell us right in our own market. The depreciation, or, in other words, the premium they get on exchange would pay duty two or three times over. There are many hon. members in the house, and some people throughout the country who still hold to the theory that the rise in retail prices which would result if our currency were depreciated would completely offset the advantage we would receive by an increase in price brought about by a premium on exchange, or in other words by a depreciation in our currency.

certainly disprove the contention that the apparent advantage which would come to Canadian farmers in cheaper currency would be offset by a rise in the prices of the things he would have to purchase.
Action such as I have suggested, that is depreciation of our currency to the level, I would suggest, of Australia, or whatever depreciation we may have, will put more money in circulation, which in turn will increase the purchasing power of the people, which will increase employment, increase trade, and as a result will increase the revenue of this government, increase railway earnings and decrease unemployment relief budgets for all our governments. I think it would enable our governments to balance their budgets. I notice in the New York Times recently that even Argentina has a balanced budget. There is a dispatch in the New York Times of October 15 from Buenos Aires saying that finance minister Hueyo announced that he would have a balanced budget ready for submission to congress this week. While we are struggling along here with high prices, "sound money", a country like Argentina with a smaller population and less natural wealth is able to balance its budget while we are faced with a deficit of probably $100,000,000 to $120,000,000. The measures which I suggest would, if adopted now before our situation becomes too desperate, save thousands of our farmers and others in Canada from bankruptcy. It would save many of our municipalities from default and would make many mortgages and bank loans and municipal debentures, which are now of very uncertain value, worth their face value.
This is a matter of interest to the whole nation. Any plans which this government may make for the employment of our people must necessitate some change in our monetary policy. I suggest to the government that when the interprovincial conference takes place, very concrete plans should be outlined for the employment of our people. I suggest that they gather the best practical men who can be found in Canada, together with some of our economists, and charge them with the duty of bringing before the government plans for the employment of our people. Unemployed people create no wealth. We have in Canada an abundance of material and natural resources, and we have people ready to work; it is simply a question of using our own credit, our own money, currency which is now printed and lying in the federal vaults, to put these people to work and produce real wealth. Let them at least produce something to provide for their own needs.

I just mention in passing the proposal which I made a year ago, that we should undertake a housing scheme, tearing down the slums in some of our big cities and building modern apartment houses. There is nothing impossible about dealing with this question of unemployment; it is just that we lack nerve to tackle it. The hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson), I am sure, knows many lumbermen who have lumber to sell and who would be glad to sell it very cheaply; and there are many people in Canada who need houses, there are many carpenters who would be glad to do the work. Let us bring the men and the material together and build these houses.
May I make one other suggestion, with special relation to my own constituency. There is a great deal of unemployment in the coal districts. I do not think that employment can be given these people at this time of year, but I suggest that the government be a little more liberal in dealing with municipalities and provinces, at least in western Canada, and as far as I am concerned in eastern Canada also, so that they may take care of these people. This correspondent of mine says that there are quite a few working on provincial relief, road work, at 30 cents an hour. The married men get ten days per month at $2.40 a day; single men get five days.
