I should like, if I may be
allowed, to complete this statement. Some men with big families get an extra day in. Then he says the union and the town council are appointing a committee to canvass the town for money for the needy. The union men working at the mine pay five per cent from their wages, but working only two days in two weeks it does not amount to much. I would urge upon the government that they deal more liberally with some of these municipalities in the west that are finding it very difficult to handle the problem on the present basis of relief.

Mr. Speaker, I should not have found
it necessary to speak this evening if the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) had acceded to the request of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and announced a definite policy regarding the subject now under discussion. In the Unemployment and Farm Relief bill introduced last session by the Prime Minister there is nothing definite as to what the policy of the government then was

Farm Finance-Mr. Vallance
in the matter of farm relief. As he was presenting the bill I asked him if it was the intention of the government to continue the five cents per bushel bonus on wheat, or if they had changed their mind and were now going to adopt an acreage basis. His reply was to the effect that they had not yet decided what the policy should be, but were taking power under the bill to do all things necessary regarding farm relief if an emergency should arise. It has been suggested to the government time and time again during this session that some pronouncement be made by them as to their relief policy. So far all we have been able to get from the Prime Minister is that he was spending money for the stabilization of the wheat market rather than paying the five cents per bushel bonus. He pointed out that it cost some $11,000,000 last year to pay the five cent bonus, and he thought that by taking that amount and stabilizing the market by the purchase of futures he would help the wheat grower more than he would by paying the bonus. There is one thing that puzzles those of us who are deeply interested in the wheat industry, and there are several on this side of the house, and some on the other side who are themselves in the industry. It is rather strange that at the very time that this government was supposed to be stabilizing the market, we find on more than one occasion that the Chicago market was higher than the Winnipeg market; and the Prime Minister said that had it not been for the intervention of the government in stabilizing the market, wheat would have gone below 40 cents per bushel. We have asked him on several occasions to tell the house and the country just how far the government has gone in this stabilizing, but we have been unable to get anything from him.
A good deal has been said to-night about the condition of western agriculture, but there is one particular condition that prevails to-day, especially in Saskatchewan, which has never been known to prevail 'before. In the old Northwest Territories we had an act that permitted the seizure of farm produce for taxes. That act has never been invoked during the twenty-seven years I have been privileged to live in that province, and I have been living on a farm throughout that entire period. The custom had always been, until this year, that when a farmer was one year delinquent in his taxes they sold a tax receipt. That is to say, they sold the land for the value of arrears of taxes and then the farmer had two years in which to redeem his land; but because of the inability of individuals or corporations to buy 53719-100J
tax receipts, the municipalities themselves found that they were the only purchasers of such receipts, and it came to the point where many municipalities were unable to carry on in this manner. They have this year had recourse to the old Northwest Territories Act and have created out of every secretary treasurer of a rural municipality a bailiff, and that official has been collecting taxes by seizing farm produce. For the first time in the twenty-seven years I have Lived in Saskatchewan we have witnessed such a procedure. That proves conclusively to those of us who are interested in the land that the land to-day has no value, simply because the produce of the land is itself without value.
I should like very briefly to outline the position of the individual who happens to live in that portion of western Canada and who had a crop this year, and to see where his money goes after he has got his crop. The first persons who have a claim on that crop are the Saskatchewan relief commission, provided that the farmer has received some relief from the commission. That comes before anything else, mortgage, interest or anything else. Following that come taxes, and the produce of the farm can be seized for taxes. After that come merchants, grocers, food mortgage. Now you have those three, and they come before even wages. What position does the farmer find himself in? The average bushelage for that portion of northern Saskatchewan that grew a crop this year was 16 bushels. I should say that the average price received by the grower was less than 30 cents-between 25 and 30 cents. To-day they are not receiving 25 cents in many parts of the west. Where there is a 26 cents freight rate per hundred pounds they are getting somewhere around 21i or 22 cents, and where there is a 24 cent rate, which is the rate in the division I live in, we are getting about 24 cents to-day.
Now, naturally the farmer who has not the equipment to thresh or to combine his crop must depend on someone else. When that someone else is approached and asked either to thresh the crop or to take it off with a combine, he naturally looks the crop over and estimates the bushelage. He may find that, after the relief commission have had their pound of flesh and the municipality has taken its taxes, and the merchant what is coming to him, there is not enough left to pay labour, and the result is that many farmers will conclude it is not worth while even taking off the crop. That is what has happened. Then the relief commission stepped in through the provincial government and announced that the

Farm Finance-Mr. Vallance
first hundred dollars' worth of crop that was taken off would be exempt from all seizure. There are a great many of these farmers today who are farming on land which they rent from the mortgage company and they deliver to the mortgage company one third of the crop, so that it is utterly impossible for these people to carry on in that part of Canada. That is why we have been impressing on this government the necessity for some definite policy, some statement as to how the government proposes to relieve agriculture, because the mental strain which is evident to-day throughout that western country is simply appalling. I think it is the duty of every member of this house to urge upon the government the absolute necessity for action, if for no other reason than to relieve the mental strain which these pioneers in western Canada are undergoing.
Let me draw a picture for you, Mr. Speaker. I said I lived in western Saskatchewan for twenty-seven years. I went there as a youth and at that time it was a wilderness, the nearest railway station being some 110 miles distant, and I have seen that country grow out of a wilderness. I have seen them build highways, railways, telegraphs, telephones, schools, towns, villages and hamlets. I have seen millions, yes billions of wealth roll out of that country in live stock and in all sorts of cereals, and in some manufactured goods; and the tragedy of the whole thing is that after twenty-seven years of effort not only on the part of the farmer himself but on the part of his wife and his family as well, he finds himself today with very little if any equity in the land which he wrested from the wilderness.
For these reasons I think this government tonight should give some ray of hope by a pronouncement of definite policy as to how they propose to relieve these people. I do not intend to read extracts from papers or letters. There is no member in this house who could not produce all manner of clippings from papers to support the argument I am putting forward. Hon. gentlemen could give all sorts of statistics from various sources. I could read letter after letter setting forth the very conditions I have depicted in the last few minutes. What I am concerned about is whether the government will take action and make some announcement which will give some ray of hope to these people.
I have been amazed that hon. gentlemen sitting behind the government, members from these western provinces, should apparently be so little interested in this matter. I listened to the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Murphy), delivering or reading an address 
some two or three weeks ago, but he had nothing concrete to put before the house. There was nothing in what he said that offered any solution of the problem. We have been waiting patiently to hear from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir). He knows the conditions in western Canada; he knows what the western agriculturist has to face. And the Prime Minister knows it just as well as any of us, for he has lived in that country for thirty-five years; I have heard him say so himself. There are many out there tonight who do not know where the next hundred pounds of coal is coming from. The other day I received a letter from my wife telling me of a neighbour who had taken fifty bushels of barley to the village of Superb with which to buy some coal. That barley netted him exactly one dollar, and I ask the house to consider how much coal could be bought for a dollar. In many parts of that country it is now twenty ibelow zero; there are two feet of snow on the ground, and many of these people do not know how they are going to live through this winter. In spite of the Prime Minister's statement that we have threshed this matter over on previous occasions, nothing has been done. The reason why we do what we are doing tonight is to impress upon this government if at all possible the absolute necessity of definite action being taken immediately. And it should not be done surreptitiously, but should be announced so that these people may at least see a little ray of hope.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey): Mr. Speaker, one almost feels like apologizing for saying again what has been said so many times in this house, but when one thinks of the condition of agriculture and the suffering of the people he welcomes an opportunity to say again and again those things which he knows to be so true. We know that the two great problems facing Canada today are the problems of unemployment and agricultural relief, and I believe there is a connection between these problems. If we can solve the problem of agriculture, if we could get agriculture into a healthy and thriving condition, it would in part solve the problem of unemployment.
May I be permitted once more to state the agricultural problem? It is this: there are three levels affecting the farmer. The first and lowest level is the level of his commodity prices. Above that is the level of the prices of the things which he must have, the things he needs in his daily life. There is a great disparity between these two. The farmer

Farm Finance-Miss Macphail
getting what he is getting at the moment for his commodities cannot buy any substantial amount of the things which are on the market and clamouring to be consumed. Above these two levels is the still higher level of debts. The farmer is required to meet his obligations and to consume goods, and if he cannot do these things, disaster faces the whole nation. As things are at the moment he simply cannot, and I think, we will have to keep repeating this fact over and over again. The farmer today cannot pay the interest upon his debts, and he cannot pay for the services and goods which he requires. It is impossible. It is certainly quite obvious that something must be done about it. Either the debt level must be scaled down closer to the commodity price level, or the commodity price level must be brought up nearer to the debt level; and also the disparity which exists today between the prices the farmer gets for the commodities he sells and the prices he has to pay for the goods which he needs must be lessened.
You can hardly take up any publication which comes into an agricultural community without finding these ideas emphasized. Just the other day the United Farmers of Ontario issued a manifesto dealing with agricultural conditions. This manifesto was sent to the clubs, the united farmers' organizations in Ontario, the municipal council and all agricultural bodies. The first paragraph reads as follows:
Ontario agriculture faces a crisis. The result of several generations of intelligent, self-sacrificing and unremitting toil is disappearing with ominous rapidity. Progressively exploited for some time past through the artificial stimulation of modern industrialism, it now faces the danger of rapid decay and general bankruptcy. Ordinarily the farmer faces a business depression, as he does other difficulties, with courage and confidence. But the situation is different today. The extent, duration and severity of the present economic breakdown have brought about a condition of hopelessness which is both a threat and a challenge to every citizen. The farmer's savings are being exhausted, and his capital is being depleted, at such a rate that the end is in sight. Municipal institutions cannot be maintained much longer on the present basis. Rural civilization is crumbling.
I should like to quote from the next paragraph as follows:
The collapse of prices destroyed the farmer's purchasing power. The inevitable result was a steady decline in merchants' sales, a falling off of wholesalers' orders, a curtailment of manufacturing output and a marked reduction in railway tonnage.
The manifesto then goes on to say that all along the line unemployment has been created. Very much the same thing is said in the Country Guide. If Mr. Speaker will
permit me I should like to read portions of an editorial which appeared in the November issue. The editorial starts off by saying that wheat prices have not been so low in fifty years, and goes on to say that other prices are also much lower. It states that with tax arrears, interest arrears and debts steadily mounting, the agricultural industry is in an extremely bad way. It then continues:
Not only is Canada's major industry facing ruin, but the lack of farm purchasing power is the direct cause of business stagnation throughout the country with a rising tide of unemployment and huge deficits being faced by municipalities, provincial governments and even by the federal government. This process of liquidation is continuing at an alarming rate with no relief in sight. It is no exaggeration to say that we are heading towards a national disaster in the midst of a world-wide disaster.
Before I came in to the chamber the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) had given the declines which had occured in the annual revenue of agriculture from 1928-29 to 1930-31, but these figures will bear repeating. The loss during these three years amounted to $925,779,000. That being true one does not need to read any manifestos issued by any agricultural body or editorials written by agricultural editors to realize that such a loss in the purchasing power of the agricultural people will cripple the whole commercial community of Canada.
If we are desirous of raising the commodity price level to a point closer to the level of the prices the farmer must pay for the things he needs and to the debt level, we must find some way of doing it. I think many of us have come to the conclusion that one of the great reasons for this disparity is Canada's remaining on the gold standard while her chief customer and her chief competitor in agricultural products have long since dropped the gold standard and inflated their currency. I sometimes wonder just how long we are going to go on bleeding the agricultural and other primary industries of Canada. I quote again from the editorial in the Country Guide, which covers almost a whole page, as follows:
If the Canadian government were to abandon the gold standard temporarily and bring our currency to the basis of the British currency, the agricultural industry of Canada would receive a stimulus beyond what could be brought about by any other method now in sight. Practically all of our important competitors in agricultural products throughout the world, except the United States have gone off the gold standard.
Then again:
Our agricultural industry would benefit decidedly and immediately if our currency were placed upon a'parity with the British pound. It would help at once to reestablish the price

Farm Finance-Miss Macphail
level between agricultural products and other commodities in Canada and would bring immediate relief to the agricultural industry which would be felt throughout the whole commercial life of Canada.
When we in this corner of the house first started to advocate inflation, the rest of the members were certainly not impressed and thought it was very wild talk. One who has been here now for some years cannot help realizing that the house is gradually and possibly quite rapidly coming to see that inflation of our currency, the putting of more money into circulation, bringing the amount of money in circulation into relation to the goods in circulation and not out of relation as it is at the moment, is a sensible thing to do. May I presume to say that it is the thing that will be done and I would not be surprised to see this government do it. Two years ago I would have said that was impossible; a year ago I would have said it was impossible, but I do not say that now. It is possible that this government will do the very thing that we have for some time been advocating.
The hon. member has a great deal of faith.

8.	Certain industries, such as the newsprint industry, which sells a large part of its output in the United States, a gold standard country, would stand to benefit materially.

May I say to the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Gordon) that I appreciate his sincerity and sympathize with his earnestness in seeking to place on the land people who are destitute. I wish for his sake as well as for theirs that the scheme would prove success-

Farm Finance-Miss Macphail
ful, but I think it cannot succeed. It is not possible to put people on the land who have been off the land for some time, and for the most part putting them on poor land, with equipment not comparable to that of their neighbours, and expect them to succeed where those much better equipped in knowledge and otherwise have failed. I do not think it is possible. I was up at North Bay two or three weeks ago and the people in the township that runs right up to the city of North Bay told me the very same story that was told to this house to-night by the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh), of families brought there from southern Ontario in the spring, without any consultation with the municipality, people who were not in any way able to take care of themselves through the winter, and who only meant an added burden upon that municipality. I really think that that movement cannot succeed.
May I add this? I was astonished to hear the Minister of Immigration deplore "the hiving," as he called it, of people in the industrial centres. I had always thought that that was the very object of the smokestack policy that we have had in Canada for almost seventy years. We have done everything possible to drive people off the land and into the cities, so do not let us complain now if the thing has been successful. It is astonishing to hear anybody who during all these years has been advocating the pampering-I cannot think of a better word

of secondary industries express pity that people are now hiving in the industrial centres. We have done veiy well to keep anybody on the land in view of all the effort made to lure them away.
There is one other thing that I want to suggest as a method of relieving the present situation, and that is the lifting of federal taxation off the backs of the masses and putting it quite firmly on the .backs of the classes. I think that federal taxation should be applied pretty largely to incomes and inheritances. We all know that the difficulty of our age is the lack of distribution of goods. There are two groups in Canada and every other country which make the distribution of goods impossible. The one is the great mass of people, at the moment the unemployed and the underprivileged, whether on the land or in the cities, who wish to consume goods but have not the money ito pay for the goods they could quite easily consume. The other class consist of those people who, by the pampering of industry and finance which we have had for so long a time, have amassed more money than they can conveniently use. So we have these two classes, one with a 
capacity to buy but unable to consume sufficient to take the goods off the market, and the other with the capacity to consume but not the purchasing power. If we lifted the burden of federal taxation off the masses and put it on the people who have now too much money for our economic good, we would I think be helping very much to solve our present problems.
Then too, I think as time goes on, particularly if science and invention continue to make the strides in the next twenty-five years which they have made in the past, we must face the fact that hours of labour must be and will be lessened, while the purchasing power of the workers is sustained. One of the things that I deplore at the moment is that wages are being beaten down all over. Even people who do not need to lower wages are lowering them. The need of the people is being used as a club over their heads. In the long run that policy will hurt not only the people who are deprived of their purchasing power, but-those who have the goods which they wish to sell. I think anybody who is thinking about the problem sees quite clearly that if we are ever going to absorb our unemployed again we must lessen the hours of labour. I think that is sound. Possibly we have not got to the place where we like to think it, but at any rate I think we are going to get to that place. If we are going to continue to give special privileges to financial and industrial groups in this country-I am speaking now particularly of industrial groups-if we are going to continue to tax all the people for the sake of certain industrial enterprises which claim to be necessary to the national life of this country, we must see to it that the benefits which they receive are passed on down both to the general consumer who buys the goods and to the worker in the factory who produces the goods. We must see that wages are sustained and working hours lessened. I see no justification for continuing to give privilege to secondary industries in this country when the mass of the people are in the distress they are in today. I think it will not be long before this house will come to the conclusion that if industries are going to be pampered and petted the benefits they receive must be passed on down by them. Markets may be saved for them, but they must pay for the saving of those markets in reduced prices and sustained wages.
The benefit of the machinery must be divided.
Will the hon. member do the same for the manufacturers?

We have always done the same for the manufacturers, if my information is correct. Not only have we loaned money which will never be repaid, but we have pampered them all the days of my life, at any rate.
Now, for the remainder of the time at my disposal-and it is not very long-I wish to discuss the problem of unemployment. I feel that what I have so far advocated in my remarks up to this point would help to absorb the unemployed. But at the moment we are faced with a terrific problem of unemployment in Canada. We have to try to do something about it. There are certain classes of unemployed which cause me more concern than others. One of these is youth. When I think that in the last generation a- great many of the youth were killed or maimed beyond repair, and that this generation of youth in quite a different way are being injured beyond repair-
Morally and physically.

Yes. Unless the despair *an be lifted from their hearts very shortly, many of them will never be the citizens they would otherwise have been. When you think that out of our schools and colleges there come about 100,000 a year, and that only a small percentage of them are finding real places in life, we come to realize the magnitude of this problem. These young people come out eager and more anxious then than at any other time to get into the adventure of life, and it is a very serious condition when they have not the opportunity to work.
We have heard lately a great deal about crime, criminals, penitentiaries, riots and that

Farm Finance-Miss Macphail
sort of thing. One of the difficulties is that we have overcrowding in our penitentiaries; there are many other things wrong. We have a penal system that is antiquated and that belongs to another age, not this one at all. But part of the trouble is due to overcrowding. The majority of people in our penitentiaries today are young people. The striving, eagerness and restlessness of youth will find an outlet, whether the policy of the government or the policy of the society in which we live will allow it a suitable outlet or not. They will find an outlet whether by quarrelling, thieving or whatever it may be. Anyone who has taught school knows you cannot have young, restless people doing nothing, and not have trouble result. It is unavoidable.
When I heard an hon. member deplore the fact that some young chap had held a gun under his nose, I concluded that such a condition was deplorable-especially if it was not the right nose. But on the other hand there is no use in blaming youth. There is no use in saying all we can do is to punish crime out of existence. That is nonsense; it cannot be done. While I believe there should be control and that there should be punishment as part of the process of reforming the individual, I believe also that punishment alone should not be resorted to. I know enough about youth to know that. Surely all of us who know young people know that the eagerness, the drive and the urge in youth will find an outlet, good or bad.
The second class that concerns me among the unemployed are the "young-o'ld" I named them myself-the people around fifty who with their experience and training and matured knowledge of life should be at the height of their usefulness. In far too many cases the unemployed are people around fifty, a disastrous age at which to make people feel useless and discouraged. Many such start the car in the garage and are found dead; or they jump into the river or take whatever seems [DOT] the best way out. At any rate they are despondent and despairing. I visited several shelters last winter, and it was one of the hardest things I have ever done, seeing people of all ages scurrying around to avoid saying a word to me, to avoid meeting me-I do not think it was just meeting me; I think it would have been the same with any hon. member who had gone there. They did not want to discuss their plight; they were ashamed, cowed, beaten. That is the worst possible thing that can happen to any group of citizens, and when it comes to the point that we must decide between the chances for youth, the

morale of great groups of our citizens, of the young-old, and finance, then it does not take me a moment to decide; I decide for humanity and human happiness, let it take what toll it will of accumulated wealth.
On motion of Mr. Ralston the debate was adjourned.
